The silhouette looks more like a candelabra or octopus shape than an oak — the limbs are too thin, sinuous, and tentacle-like, lacking the thick, slow-tapering, angular branching typical of real oak limbs.

I'm also spotting a base issue: the trunk's bulb disc extends below the ground crest line, poking into the brown ground as a visible gray-black blob since the trunk color reads darker than the dirt. I need to fix this by repainting the ground over that overflow, but honestly the whole tree looks crude enough that I should rethink the approach entirely.

Looking at how Friedrich actually painted oaks — in "Abbey in the Oakwood" the trunks are thick and short with heavy twisted limbs splitting into fine branch filigree, some broken and dead; in "Oak Tree in Snow" the trunk is massive and hollow with spreading thick limbs. My current limbs are too long, smooth, and taper too thin — I should redesign with thicker primary limbs (30-60 width) that fork more aggressively into shorter, heavier branches following the rule that child diameters squared sum to roughly the parent's squared, giving a much stockier, more irregular silhouette than what I have now.

I'm sketching concrete coordinates now: a crooked trunk around 76 units wide at the base near (244, 530), tapering as it rises before forking near y≈440, with the overall crown forming a wide irregular dome spanning roughly x=30 to x=560, its main limbs splaying outward at 30–60° from vertical.

Checking proportions against real oak trees — trunk-to-crown ratio looks close to natural (1:10-1:13) — then starting to plot primary limb paths point by point from the fork, but realizing hand-designing dozens of limbs this way is tedious and considering a more systematic approach instead.

Rather than manually placing each limb, I'll build a deterministic secondary-branching generator that sprouts thicker side limbs at wide angles using filled body masks rather than thin lines. Each child limb gets a crooked spine and a width scaled from its parent's local width (roughly 0.55-0.7x at the joint, tapering to about 1.5 at the tip), painted with a pointed brush stroke that tapers from full width down to about 22% of it.

I'm thinking thick forking limbs (orders 1-3) should use the body-mask approach for crooked, organic shapes following an area rule, while finer twig masses (orders 4-6) use the lighter stroke-based recursion — giving me separate brush sizes (small, medium, large) for different limb thicknesses.

Now I'm designing a procedural limb generator with randomized spine segments, periodic forking where child branches split off at varying angles with widths following the area-conservation rule, and a slight upward bias so limbs naturally curve skyward over successive segments.

I'm weighing how much to hand-specify versus let randomness handle: I'll treat randomness as part of my drawing process, specifying primary limbs by hand while letting the generator fill in secondary growth and twigs. Given the tree is the central subject and I have budget to spare, I decide to invest carefully in getting the painting process right, starting by covering the trunk base crest with wet ground paint before laying down the trunk itself.

Now I'm pinpointing the bulb region's coordinates to know exactly where to repaint, then planning to construct the new trunk as a polygon with a slight lean, twist, and root flare spreading into the ground.

Plotting trunk outline points...

Tracing the crest line around y≈526 near the trunk, I realize the trunk base should overlap the ground slightly, and I'm comparing the trunk's dark umber-black mix against the ground's warmer brown tones so I can blend the trunk to terminate right at the crest without a harsh value jump.

For the trunk-ground junction, I should clip the trunk mask against the ground polygon so they never overlap, then paint any root flares directly onto the ground using a separate root-shaped mask in dark color. For planning the limb network, I'm considering sketching the skeleton in pencil on the dry paint first as a guide, since graphite won't disturb the surface and can be painted over afterward.

Though I realize pencil lines left visible in sky gaps between branches would be a problem if the design shifts, and erasing them risks a ghost mark, while there's no real preview tool. So I'll just have to commit to a careful design upfront, accepting that fixing mistakes would mean redoing a section of sky.

Building the tree gradually makes more sense: add limbs easily, but removing them is hard, so I should start conservative. Looking at what's painted so far — trunk, central and side limbs with elbows, low branches — the silhouette is reading too much like an octopus because the limbs are smooth and long. I'll add thicker bridging elements, secondary limbs with elbows, and more mass in the crown to break up that look and add structure.

The wavy S-curve of the central limb is also a problem since real oak limbs zigzag at junctions rather than flowing like seaweed, and the tips taper too fast into thin wands. I'm planning to add strong secondary branches at wide angles along each primary limb, walking along each spine and spawning new growth at intervals to build out a denser, more tree-like branch mesh.

Writing branch generator code...

I'm also figuring out how to compute local position, direction, and width along a parent polyline at a given arclength, and deciding to paint thicker limbs with body-hand masks while thinner twigs get pointed brush strokes based on pressure per width.

I'm setting up brush size classes for different widths and deciding to taper strokes with linear pressure ramps between endpoint widths.

For thicker limbs I'd prefer body_of bark-outline shapes over simple strokes to give a more natural woody silhouette, reserving plain tapered strokes for finer twigs. But really the core issue is that my primary limbs read as tentacles rather than oak branches -- they're too long, smooth, and uniformly tapered. function oakshoot2(x, y, ang, len, w0, depth, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local pts = {{x, y}}
  local angs = {}
  local cx, cy, a = x, y, ang
  local used = 0
  local kink = opts.kink or 0.5
  while used < len do
    local l = math.min(rand(opts.lmin or 8, opts.lmax or 16), len - used)
    if l < 3.0 then break end
    a = a + rand(-kink, kink)
    cx = cx + math.cos(a) * l
    cy = cy + math.sin(a) * l
    used = used + l
    pts[#pts+1] = {cx, cy}
    angs[#angs+1] = a
  end
  if #pts < 2 then return end
  local w1 = math.max(0.87, w0 * 0.3)
  tw:load(OakT, 1.0)
  tw:stroke(pts, {pressure={tw:pressure_for(math.max(w0, 0.9)), tw:pressure_for(w1)}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  if depth > 0 then
    local total = used
    local d = 0
    for i = 2, #pts do
      d = d + math.sqrt((pts[i][1]-pts[i-1][1])^2 + (pts[i][2]-pts[i-1][2])^2)
      if math.random() < (opts.p or 0.6) then
        local side = (math.random() < 0.5) and 1 or -1
        local sa = angs[i-1] + side * rand(0.4, 0.95)
        local rem = total - d
        local sl = math.max(7, (rem + rand(5, 16)) * rand(0.45, 0.85))
        oakshoot2(pts[i][1], pts[i][2], sa, sl, math.max(0.9, w0 * 0.75), depth - 1, opts)
      end
    end
  end
end
function sprout3(name, from, to, spacing, wcap, depth, lenmin, lenmax, opts)
  local L = OAK[name]
  local pts, wd = L[1], L[2]
  local s = {0}
  for i = 2, #pts do
    s[i] = s[i-1] + math.sqrt((pts[i][1]-pts[i-1][1])^2 + (pts[i][2]-pts[i-1][2])^2)
  end
  local total = s[#pts]
  local pos = total * from
  local flip = (math.random() < 0.5) and 1 or -1
  while pos < total * to do
    local i = 1
    while i < #pts-1 and s[i+1] < pos do i = i + 1 end
    local t = (pos - s[i]) / (s[i+1] - s[i])
    local px = pts[i][1] + t * (pts[i+1][1]-pts[i][1])
    local py = pts[i][2] + t * (pts[i+1][2]-pts[i][2])
    local la = math.atan(pts[i+1][2]-pts[i][2], pts[i+1][1]-pts[i][1])
    local wl = wd[i] + t * (wd[i+1]-wd[i])
    local sa = la + flip * rand(0.35, 0.85)
    flip = -flip
    oakshoot2(px, py, sa, rand(lenmin, lenmax), clamp(wl * 0.42, 0.9, wcap), depth, opts)
    pos = pos + spacing * rand(0.7, 1.3)
  end
end

Before the talus addition, it had a convincing alpenglow face with a darker shadow side and visible strata, reading as a proper rock tower — the bell-shaped talus made it too wide and building-like. I think the fix is to simplify back to a narrower sandstone massif with vertical cliffs disappearing into fog, like Lilienstein, and repaint fog color over the talus edges outside the cliff column to restore that cleaner silhouette.

Now I need to rework the value structure overall: the butte should read darkest at the top and lighten toward the hazy base, with the shadow face clearly darker than the lit face, but right now everything sits at too similar a lilac-gray value because my base color and shadow layer aren't contrasting enough.

I'll strengthen the shadow face with a darker, cooler mix (umber, smalt, Prussian, touch of white) painted at higher coverage, keep the lit face warmer and lighter, and place the vertical ridge edge slightly right of center so the lit face reads wider. Then I'll blend the faces vertically, soften the base into the fog with ragged edges, and tuck small dark tree dabs along the cliff foot ledges to tie into the fog below.

I'll work this as one wet-in-wet session since the butte paint is still fresh, defining the column mask from the existing cliff shape, then covering the skirt with warm-tinted fog strokes that blend seamlessly into the surrounding mist without visible patch edges.

I'll test a soft-edged skirt cover using a filbert brush with coverage 4, avoiding the clip option so the edge dissolves naturally, then move on to modeling the cliff column's shadow face with strong value contrasts — though I should reconsider whether the butte really reads best as a column form.

Actually, a more natural silhouette would have an irregular contour with ledges and a slightly concave profile, plus talus slopes at the base fading into fog. Since the fog will bury the lower portion anyway, I can keep the cliff walls vertical down to a certain height, then let a 45-degree talus slope widen outward before dissolving into the haze.

The bell shape makes geometric sense for real butte profiles, but mine came out too steep, too wide, and too abruptly flat-lit, so I want a subtler flare—widening only modestly on each side and fogging over more of that skirt starting partway down. Rather than reworking the talus itself, I'll just lean on a heavier fog bank across the whole base with soft horizontal wisps to obscure the excess width.

Now I'm planning the execution in two passes: first modelling the cliff column itself with deeper shadow on the right, relaying the warm lit face, and adding ragged dabs of trees at the cliff foot in a mid-dark tone for contrast; then laying in the fog bank with opaque horizontal strokes over the base.

I'm mixing a dark blue-brown shadow color and an even deeper near-black umber-prussian mix for the lower-right edge, planning to apply shadow coverage first and deepen it at the edges, accounting for the wet underlayer lightening the new strokes as they blend.

The warm mix is too weak and blotchy since it's mixing wet into the BCool2 layer underneath. I think the better approach is patience: let each wet layer dry fully (several days given the slow-drying umber and lead white) before applying the next, rather than rushing the sequence.

So I'll wait a week, then tackle the shadow and lit faces with strong opaque values first, add the tree dabs next, and finish with the fog layer.

-- gullies & buttresses: irregular vertical ribbons, hand-placed
function gully(x0, y0, y1, wob, w0, w1, seed)
  local pts, ws = {}, {}
  local n = math.max(3, math.floor((y1-y0)/10))
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    pts[#pts+1] = {x0 + wob*math.sin(i*1.3 + seed) + rand(-0.7,0.7), y0 + (y1-y0)*t}
    ws[#ws+1] = w0 + (w1-w0)*t
  end
  return ribbon(pts, ws)
end

That blending just flattened the lit and shadow faces into a uniform warm-gray, and the gullies now read as too regular and graphic, like drips on a candle — this is worse than before. The butte remains the weakest part despite many passes, so I need to step back and reconsider how a sandstone tabletop mountain like Lilienstein actually reads at a distance before trying again.

At several kilometers out, detail softens into broad planes: a dark forest cap on a flat top, vertical cliffs with subtle horizontal banding, irregular fissures that start at the top edge and fade rather than running the full height, and bases lost in forest and fog. My mistake was making the gullies too uniform and parallel with rounded ends, when real fissures are irregular, branching, and vary in tone. Instead of lines, I should try stippling or dry-brush texture to create rock-like mottling — clustering warm light and cool dark tones with vertical drag to suggest the stratification more naturally.

The butte also feels too dominant and competes with the oak — I want to push it back visually by making it paler, bluer, and softer like the distant mountains in Friedrich's work, with less saturation and a subtler glow instead of strong orange light. Raising the fog line so only the top of the cliff peeks above it, like a small island in a sea of mist, would reduce its visual weight and make it read as a secondary, more atmospheric element.

I'm also rethinking its proportions — making it wider than tall (a flat mesa rather than a tall column) feels more elegant and distant-looking, so burying the lower half in fog around y≈405 would create that tabletop effect while keeping it consistent with the fog level near the horizon and the far ridge line.

Thickening the fog locally around the butte's base, say to y≈420, gives a visible height of about 88 units against a 140-unit width, which reads well as mesa-like. For the surface, I'm softening the lit face into a muted pinkish-lilac-brown and the shadow face into a mid-value lilac-blue-gray, and smoothing away the stripes with subtle blending.

Then I'm adding sparse irregular fissures with a fine rigger brush at low contrast, plus faint horizontal strata bands with ragged edges and small tree tufts on ledges. Actually, since the surface is still wet, I think it's better to fully repaint the butte with a fresh opaque coat applied wet-in-wet, keeping detail minimal: a base layer of lilac-gray (lead white, smalt, red earth, raw umber, yellow ochre) painted in vertical strokes across the masked column, followed by a darker shadow plane on the right side.

Then I'll add a lit plane on the left side with warm tones fading downward, softly blend the arete where the two planes meet, and finish with a scumbled texture layer to suggest rocky mottling.

Next I'm planning fissures as thin irregular dark lines with branching, small foliage dabs clustered along ledge lines, and a fog layer with a ragged gradient top over the lower portion—while noting the alpenglow face needs warmer treatment on the left side.

Since the butte sits nearer than the sun, the face we see should actually be in shadow, not lit — the butte should read as a dark silhouette with only a warm rim-light along its left edge, which fits the Friedrich-style composition better than a fully sunlit face.

Since the light hits at a grazing angle, the lit face shouldn't be too saturated or bright — I'll keep it below the sky's value, maybe around 0.6-0.65, a muted salmon tone. The butte sits at mid-distance beyond the fog bank, so aerial perspective calls for value ~0.45 on the shadow face and ~0.6 on the lit face, while keeping the existing silhouette with its needle, tower, step, and forest crown details.

Since the wet layers need to dry before I add more, I'll wait 7 days and use that time productively on independent areas — foreground grasses, the oak's bark and rim light (which is now dry enough to work on), and the right foreground spruces and rock. I'll start with the oak's trunk, building up its dark brown-black silhouette using a mix of umber, Prussian blue, bone black, and red earth.

Thinking about the bark's fine structure now — Friedrich's oaks have deep vertical furrows, warm-lit on the side facing light, which comes from the right and behind in this scene. I'm uncertain whether the `offset` mask function shifts position or dilates/erodes the shape, so I'm reasoning through how to test it empirically before relying on it for the rim-light crescent.

events.name: look
events.text: size 1000

Looking critically at the whole image, the oak silhouette and branching structure work well, the sky gradient has a nice luminous shift from blue to peach, and the figure and fog add scale and depth. But I'm noticing the trunk base has an odd rounded bulb shape where it overlaps the ground that needs fixing.

The butte is a bigger problem — it reads as a floating mesa rather than a mountain emerging from mist, with a too-regular talus skirt, a hard white edge at its base, and overly dark, uniform drip-like gullies. I need to integrate it better with stronger atmospheric haze overlapping its lower half, a more irregular silhouette, and softer, less uniform gully shading.

I'm also picturing it more like a Saxon Switzerland sandstone tabletop (Lilienstein-style): steep striated walls, a forested talus slope at the base partly obscured by mist. The dark vertical ribbons currently look like paint drips, so I should paint over them with the face colors and replace them with subtler, form-following weathering marks instead of straight dark lines, keeping the distinctive tabletop shape rather than simplifying to a generic pyramid peak.

Looking at how Friedrich renders distant rock peaks in "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog" — pale, soft-edged, veiled in mist with minimal detail — I want to lighten and cool the butte with a translucent haze layer over the whole form, keeping the crown trees as dark but slightly veiled silhouettes and desaturating the pink lit face. I also need to redo the talus slope, since the earlier fog overpaint left an odd bell-shaped hard edge; I'll rebuild soft, irregular fog layers over the lower half and sides so the base dissolves naturally into mist.

I'm also noticing the bell's outline needs softening with overlapping fog patches and some dark tree crowns fading into the mist along the slopes, while the thin cloud bar and top sky read fine as is. The bigger issue is the lower-right fog sea, which is too flat and pale — almost snowy — pulling the eye away; I think I need to add a dark descending foreground mass or spruce trees there to balance the composition.

I'm thinking a triangular composition would balance things: oak on the left, spruces at the lower right, figure center-left, and the butte at right-middle. Planting two or three spruces of varying heights there could anchor that corner against the empty fog.

The spruce/oak contrast also works symbolically—the evergreen reads as hope or eternal life against the dead oak's mortality theme, which reinforces Friedrich's style. I'm also checking the ridge banding on the left, confirming the figure's scale feels right without a hat (staying true to the wanderer motif), and now looking at the glow near the horizon under the oak's branches.

Overall the piece reads pleasing but a bit too clean and illustrative—getting closer to Friedrich would mean adding subtler touches like thin horizontal cloud streaks and softer mist, maybe finishing with a unifying light glaze. That leads me to a priority list: fix the trunk base so it isn't swallowed by the ground and add roots/grass tufts, soften and re-veil the butte while removing the drip artifacts and restoring fog at its base, add spruces and the dark knoll at lower right, and bring in foreground grass texture with rigger strokes along the crest silhouette.

I'll skip adding birds since Friedrich rarely used them and it risks feeling kitschy, though a couple tiny crows could be considered. Starting with the trunk fix, I need to check the exact crest line coordinates near the base to paint the ground correctly through the bulb and add flaring roots.

The trunk base extends about 30 units below the crest line, which is why it currently reads as floating in front of the foreground rather than embedded in it. I'll paint the ground contour across the trunk at roughly y≈538–545, slightly below the crest, so the lower trunk gets hidden and some dark root forms can spread out visibly above the ground line.

I'll define a soil mound mask with a curved boundary covering the area below the trunk, paint it with the ground mix, then add 5–6 tapered dark roots radiating from the trunk base plus small grass tufts to anchor it naturally. After that I need to revisit the butte and examine its pink-lit left half more closely.

The butte's gray right half, drips, and pale skirt currently read as a distinct pedestal with a sharp bottom edge, so I want to obscure that boundary by layering soft fog banks over the lower half using semi-transparent cool and warm piles, letting the cliff base dissolve rather than show a hard line.

Alternatively, I could simplify the whole butte into a distant bluish mass by applying a light haze over both lit and shaded faces to flatten contrast, while keeping the pink alpenglow accent at the top-left since that Friedrich-style touch works well—the real problem areas are just the drips and that too-defined skirt.

Let me get a closer crop of the butte region to properly assess its current state before deciding which approach to take.

The butte reads as a stage prop, so I need to rethink it in a more Friedrich-like way — distant rocks as simple dark silhouettes with soft, increasingly pale edges, no internal modeling, just a subtle value gradient with fog at the base and light at the top.

I'll make it a cool, mid-value bluish-lilac mass with a warm tint on the left edge where it catches light, since the sun is low and to the left. The shape needs to be more irregular — a stepped ledge on the left, an overhang and broken pinnacle on the right, a slightly sloping top, tiny trees along the ridge, and a talus skirt dissolving into fog at the base — replacing the current flat-topped rectangle with its unnaturally straight vertical sides.

Given the haze between us and the butte, I should keep contrast moderate rather than stark. The trickiest part is erasing the old rectangular geometry and dark drips cleanly — I'll likely need to repaint the whole butte and talus in stages, first restoring the fog field underneath, then layering in the new irregular silhouette so it fully covers the old shape without leaving visible seams against the complex cream/lilac gradient around it.

I'm working out the exact wall geometry — keeping the top edge with its needle, tower, and step intact, then plotting the left and right walls with ledges, notches, and buttresses that transition into talus slopes merging with the forest on either side.

Given the time I've invested, I'm deciding to focus effort where it matters most: the butte is the painting's weakest element, so rather than tweak it, I'll rebuild it properly — first repainting soft fog banks behind the talus base, then re-modeling the wall with opaque, cool, drip-free paint and a clear backlit tonal structure.

I'm settling on a simpler Friedrich-style silhouette: flat blue-gray-violet with a subtle gradient (darker top, paler fog-washed base), warm rim light on the left edge, faint horizontal strata, and a forest crown—reading as a distant hazy sandstone form. For the repaint, I'll lay down the cool body color as a vertical gradient opaquely, then add a warm lit band along the left edge.

Next I need the lit edge to fade softly downward and blend into a right-side shadow gradient, avoiding any hard vertical line at the arete—using blurred masks and blended wet paint to keep the lit-to-shadow transition gradual, with fog banks layered over the base afterward.

For the talus, I'm scrapping the bell shape in favor of a lumpy forested slope: I'll place the fog top near y≈470-490 around the butte, paint dark-blue-green forest crowns of varied size above that line fading into wisps of fog below it, replacing the overly pale haze I'd used before, then move on to the wall.

The wall's base around y~430 should transition into that forest with a ragged treeline edge, the forest reading darker and cooler than the wall itself, plus a pale glow band at the horizon behind the butte. I'll tackle this rebuild in stages, starting with the wall.

Now I'm thinking about how to actually get a good right half using robust methods: either use fill=false with high coverage so load_at modulations still work without gaps, or use soft blurred masks with clip=true so strokes near the mask's edge get weighted paint based on the mask value, giving a soft transition rather than a hard cutoff — similar to what worked with my earlier blurred ellipse glazes.

I realize my mistake was using a binary rect mask instead of a soft one, which caused paint to fill the full region rather than fading with the gradient. With fill=true, dabs get placed into gaps wherever the mask exceeds a threshold, so a truly soft mask should let the underlying wet blending taper naturally rather than flooding the area uniformly like in the sky layer attempts.

I'm noticing the butte's base looks off: there's an odd lighter band partway down and the bottom edge is cutting off hard with a ragged tree-line instead of fading like intended, so the soft-down blending isn't actually working there.

I think I need a different approach — instead of relying on mask weighting for the fade, I should try wet-in-wet blending or glaze the fog color over the base in several thin, successively smaller passes to build a convincing atmospheric fade.

Actually, stippling might be the better physical match: tiny dabs of fog-cream paint with coverage thinning out downward would read as mist more naturally than a hard-edged gradient. My plan now is to fix the ugly pasted trapezoid at the butte's foot by reconsidering the mesa's base geometry first.

The current trapezoid looks too artificial, like a lampshade. A better approach is to let the cliff walls continue straight down with slight widening, dissolving into stippled fog rather than a solid shape, echoing the ragged forest-edged slopes in Friedrich's rock peaks. I'd need to repaint that whole trapezoid area—first covering it with an opaque cream fog coat, letting it dry, then rebuilding the butte walls properly on top.

Stepping back, though, the real issue might be the butte itself reading as too prominent and warm-toned for something meant to sit far at the horizon. Making it smaller, bluer, and hazier with less contrast—more of a dark silhouette with a lit rim rather than detailed orange-faced rock—would help it recede naturally like the distant peaks in the Wanderer painting.

Rethinking the base of the butte, I want it to plunge directly into a soft fog edge rather than having a talus slope, mimicking peaks rising from a sea of fog. That means repainting below the fog line as opaque mist and letting the lower butte fade into it through stippling, matching that classic Friedrich composition where foreground rock gives way to a fog sea with mountains emerging above it.

Actually, since the talus paint I just laid is still wet, covering it now with the cream fog would mix and muddy the color. I should let it dry for a few days before overpainting, and use that time to work out what the butte itself should look like.

Mapping it out: a flat-topped silhouette with a needle spire at the left rising higher and a tower at the right with a stepped edge, vertical walls flaring slightly outward as they descend, split along the arete into a warm lit face on the left and a cool shadowed face on the right, dissolving into wispy fog streaks near the base where it meets the ground.

To dissolve the foot into fog, I'm stippling cream tones with coverage growing from none at the top of the transition zone to near-full lower down, feathering the edges and masking to the butte's silhouette so the granular touches read as a mottled drybrush fade, with a horizontal glaze streak added for atmosphere. After letting that dry, I plan to recover the talus/lowSoft area with opaque cream clipped hard to its shape, growing the mask slightly so the boundary against the existing fog blends invisibly since they share the same color.

The full fix sequence I'm settling on: wait several days, cover the talus opaquely, wait again, repaint the butte's lower body with a hard cutoff, then stipple fog over the bottom strip with graded coverage plus a few glaze wisps to finish the blend.

But it strikes me I could combine the fog cover and butte repaint into one wet-in-wet pass — letting the cream color mix into the butte paint would naturally produce that grayish-lilac misty blend I actually want at the base, as long as I'm careful that darker strokes don't drag and smear the lighter wash underneath.

So once the earlier layer dries, my plan is: paint the fog cover opaque, then the lower butte with weighted strokes, then blend the foot region while still wet so cream and lilac fuse into a soft gradient — similar colors blending well, unlike the earlier mistake of blending over dark wet rock. While waiting for that to dry I can work on unrelated independent areas like the foreground grass.

The oak's rim light and the hump's seam also need their own dry/wet timing independent of the butte, but since time passes for the whole canvas at once with a wait call, I should use this window to do foreground work, being careful not to overlap the fresh butte paint. One task is covering a stray blue line along the crest edge by repainting it with dark foreground earth paint, masked to that specific region near the test swatch rectangles whose bottoms are bleeding into the crest.

That should cover the stray blue line once dry. Next I should add foreground grass tufts along the crest with warm ochre/umber, rim-lit blades mixed with darker shade blades, plus a few stones and stipple detail to break up the overly flat dark mass at the bottom. The oak can stay a pure silhouette without rim light, and the figure is already fine as is.

Now I'm working out the rendering approach for the grass blades themselves — thin tapered rigger strokes from base to tip, curved slightly, with backlit blades near the crest rendered in a lighter warm value against the darker ground beneath them, while blades silhouetted against the glow stay much darker in contrast.

I'm planning the actual blade generation: clusters along the crest and lower slope, each tuft containing several blades of varying height and lean, with a slight lateral curve drawn as base-mid-tip points, and distinguishing near-black silhouetted blades above the crest from the warmer rim-lit ones below it.

Still writing tuft function...

I should reload the rigger every few blades since each stroke deposits most of its load at the start and runs dry quickly with 480 strokes. For the dark silhouetted blades above the crest line, I'm mixing a dark pile of raw umber, bone black, and Prussian blue, while separately handling rim-lit blades below the crest.

I need to avoid placing tufts near the oak's roots and the figure's feet, skipping roughly x 170-350 and x 404-440. For the foreground corners, I'm planning taller dark grass clumps (h≈40-60) as silhouettes against the lighter soil in the middle ground.

Some of these blades could catch a warm backlit glow at the edges instead of staying fully dark, giving a few tall stems and seed heads in the lower-left corner (x 20-150, y 640-714) that classic Friedrich-style foreground detail. I'm also considering tall weeds silhouetted against the pale fog at the lower-right crest edge (around x 800-1000), maybe 5-7 stems, since that contrast would read well for depth.

Now I need to pin down the exact coordinates for the crest line based on the crop ratio, converting the blue line's pixel position into image units so I know precisely where to paint the foreground cover along the crest from roughly x=743 to x=918.

That small overlap keeps the crest's profile looking smooth rather than jagged.

gb = brush{kind="rigger", width=2, point=1}
function blade(bx, by, h, lean, pile_, w)
  local ang = -1.5708 + lean
  local mx = bx + math.cos(ang - lean*0.35) * h * 0.55
  local my = by + math.sin(ang - lean*0.35) * h * 0.55
  local tx = bx + math.cos(ang) * h
  local ty = by + math.sin(ang) * h
  gb:load(pile_, 0.75)
  gb:stroke({{bx,by},{mx,my},{tx,ty}}, {pressure={w or 0.55, 0.04}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
end
function tuft(x, ybase, n, hmax, pile_, lean0, spread, w)
  for i = 1, n do
    blade(x + rand(-spread, spread), ybase + rand(-1.2, 1.2), hmax * rand(0.35, 1.0), (lean0 or 0) + rand(-0.55, 0.55), pile_, w)
  end
end

function blade2(bx, by, h, lean, pile_, wmax)
  -- a curved, tapering blade: starts near vertical, bends to the lean side
  local n = 5
  local pts = {}
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    local bend = lean * t * t * 1.8
    local x = bx + math.sin(bend) * h * t + lean * 0.0
    local y = by - math.cos(bend) * h * t
    pts[#pts+1] = {x, y}
  end
  g3:load(pile_, 0.8)
  g3:stroke(pts, {pressure={wmax or 0.55, 0.05}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
end
function tuft2(x, ybase, n, hmax, pile_, lean0, spread, wmax)
  for i = 1, n do
    local side = (math.random() < 0.5) and -1 or 1
    blade2(x + rand(-spread, spread), ybase + rand(-1.0, 1.0), hmax * rand(0.3, 1.0), (lean0 or 0) + side*rand(0.1, 0.6), pile_, wmax)
  end
end
-- fine dark blades fanning from the existing tufts, against the sky/fog
for i = 1, 40 do
  local x = rand(6, 990)
  if not ((x > 150 and x < 372) or (x > 398 and x < 446)) then
    tuft2(x, crestY(x) + 1.5, math.random(5, 9), rand(10, 24), grassDark, 0.0, 6, 0.5)

events.text: size 1000

The right side is messy right now, with that fog-white block and awkward butte skirt shape clashing with the swatch rectangles. I need to rework it into a proper misty valley scene—a gradient sea of fog with the butte emerging from it, wooded humps poking through at the edge, and faint distant ridges beyond.

Using soft value-masked paint strokes rather than hard-edged blends should create natural fades, but I'm running into a problem: the forest foot area looks mottled and blue-gray instead of forest-like, and it creates a visible seam where it meets the cliff above. I need a cleaner approach to blend that transition and make the vegetation read correctly.

With the valley's opaque fog coat done, I'm stepping back to assess the whole scene critically: the left side with the oak silhouette, glowing sky gradient, and small readable figure is working well, but the butte still reads as a boxy flat-topped tower with an odd mottled skirt rather than a natural sandstone formation. I'm considering reshaping it with a more irregular, Lilienstein-like outline and steeper cliff faces to break up the current boxiness.

I'm also noticing the large empty fog expanse to the right and below the butte reads too flat and bright, almost like a snow field rather than atmospheric fog with depth — I should rebuild the earlier dome and hump shapes that gave that area structure before they got overpainted, while keeping some darker variation in the fog itself.

I'm planning to rebuild this section in layers from far to near: a horizon-level ridge, then nearer wooded humps rising from the mist, each painted wet-on-dry with soft-edged transitions so the fog reads as layered depth rather than a flat void.

I should avoid the mottled "cracks" texture that comes from painting thin, light coverage over a dry darker ground — it breaks into a lattice-like pattern instead of a smooth gradient, so I need to lay the talus with more even, soft coverage to prevent that lattice effect at the cliff's base.

Maybe stippling with feathered edges is the answer — granular touches of pale pigment in decreasing density upward, mimicking Friedrich's own grainy mist technique, since dry stipples can't blend but stay separate like a natural veil.

I'm also reconsidering the glaze approach: earlier the haze over the midreg used a thin medium-glaze with load ramps and produced a genuinely smooth veil, so maybe that's more reliable for the butte mist than stippling, which risks looking mottled rather than atmospheric.

Now I'm planning the minimal fix for the right side: paint fog-colored coverage over the talus trapezoid and the mid-cliff below y≈420 to erase the skirt, letting the fog edge rise smoothly to around y≈425 so the butte reads as a rock island poking out of the mist, with visible height roughly 95px against a 130px width.

I realize that boxy silhouette looks artificial since the walls are straight and vertical with a flat top -- I should flare the base slightly for talus, break the top with a couple of pinnacles and notches, and add gullies, horizontal strata lines, and vertical light/dark streaks for surface texture, since the earlier attempts at these got overpainted during the rebuild.

I'm weighing whether to restore some restrained surface detail -- darker shadow crevices, lit ledges, stepped ledges with small trees, a forest-top line, and a distinct dark talus fading into fog -- versus pushing the butte further toward Friedrich's style by making it smaller, paler, hazier, and lower-contrast like the distant bluish-grey peaks in Wanderer.

The current orange/pink saturation on the lit face is too cartoonish, even though Friedrich sometimes used alpenglow pinks. My cleaner plan: redo the butte as a smaller, hazier formation with a cool lilac-blue cliff body (darker than the fog, lighter than the oak tree), a subtle warm tint only on the left face, strong grading toward lighter values near the base, a dark forested talus merging into fog on both sides, and an irregular tree-dotted silhouette on top. Now I need to figure out how to rework the existing paint in that region to match this plan.

Since I'll be repainting the whole cliff opaquely over the existing orange gradient, I'm sketching a more natural hand-drawn silhouette—taller, with a notched top around y=330-340, slightly leaning walls with irregular steps, and a flared talus base extending down to about y=455 where it meets the fog. I'm positioning the butte with the left wall running from x=742 at the top down to about x=735, flaring out to x=700 as it becomes talus, and the right wall mirroring from x=868 flaring to x=915, with the talus itself rendered as a forested slope.

Now I'm adding a ragged dark tree-line along the cliff base around y=405-420, depicted as speckled clusters against the lighter rock face, with the talus edges curving concavely outward into the fog at y≈470. I'm also working out how the fog's top edge should behave—rising near the butte to about y=470 but climbing toward y=410-420 further away, eventually reaching all the way up to the distant ridge so the valley reads as fully fog-filled, consistent with the humps emerging from mist on the left side.

I'm mapping out the depth order for the right valley: the lilac far ridge, then cream fog, then the mid-distance butte rising from y≈470 to 335, then another fog bank, then the darker wooded humps emerging around y 480-560, then a nearer lilac fog layer, then the foreground slope. Since the humps sit lower in the picture plane than the butte's base yet read as closer to the viewer, I'm confirming that's consistent with perspective—so my painting order should place the butte first at full height, then layer the fog bank over its base, before adding the nearer humps on top.

To avoid lattice artifacts between layers, I'm favoring opaque paint with high coverage and gradients built through `load_at` ramps rather than mask softness, since an earlier version using `load_at` in a hill function gave a clean dark-to-fog gradient without lattice issues because the underlying fog value matched. That same approach worked for the mist coat over dry hills too, though in some cases it produced hard rectangular edges where the mask had a hard left boundary.

I'm tracing why the fogB case still shows a visible hard edge even with a smoothstep ramp in `load_at` -- the mask rect itself is hard-edged with clip=true, so paint should stop exactly at that boundary, but I suspect `load_at` actually controls the pile load per dip rather than true opacity, meaning lower load still leaves some residual paint rather than fading cleanly to nothing.

I realize the key issue: load_at is likely sampled only at the start of each stroke, not continuously along its path, so a long stroke (up to 170 units) beginning in a high-load zone keeps depositing full-strength paint well past the ramp into the low-load zone -- which explains why short strokes show smooth gradients but long ones create hard edges.

So I'm weighing two approaches: multiplying a rectangle by a soft mask for coverage-weighted softness, which gives gentler transitions but can look thin and mottled near edges, versus using an edge-loss parameter that mimics a lightly-loaded brush fading naturally past the boundary. I should test whether a "lost" or "soft" edge setting on the fog bank's top combines well with the hug behavior, and consider whether a separate function that drags a thin stroke across the mask's boundary from outside in would produce a more natural fade.

I think the cleanest path is to paint the fog's transition zone wet-in-wet during the same session as the valley, keeping the butte and humps dry underneath, then blend within that soft band while everything's still wet rather than relying purely on mask math.

This confirms the approach worked for clouds too, dragging paint upward as a thin veil over dry rock. So the plan is: paint each form opaquely on dry ground, let it dry, then paint the fog bank opaque and immediately blend across its top edge with a wide vertical blend band.

The key fix from earlier failures: restrict the blend mask tightly to the edge area so it only moves the fresh wet fog paint, leaving all the dry layers underneath untouched—unlike before when I accidentally blended a hard rectangle that dragged wet rock paint along with it. Now I want to reconsider the foreground-fog test swatches I'd set up earlier.

Those pale blue-gray rectangles are still showing faintly through the fog coat, so I need to fully paint over them with opaque fog at high coverage. Then I'll lay out the right valley butte: defining its silhouette, then building up base cliff color, shadow gradient, a warm lit edge on the left side, and finer surface details in sequence.

Adding gullies, ledges, and highlight details, then tree-lines and the dark stippled talus forest at the base blending into the fog. After letting that dry, I'll add the second fog bank covering the butte base, then move on to the remaining humps and their fog, accounting for multi-day drying waits between each thick paint layer.

Before tackling the butte, I'm checking whether the fog repaint has dried enough, noting the visible square edges still need a third fog coat in cool gray-lilac for the lower right region, transitioning warmer toward the horizon glow.

I want to add darker wooded hill silhouettes (B/E/F) peeking through the fog for depth, plus horizontal wispy streaks painted as stretched-noise glazes, and I'm thinking through how to balance the richer right side against the oak-dominated left by sketching rough positions for each hump.

The old hill C behind the oak at the left crest stays as is. I notice the left flank of dome B has an abrupt vertical edge near x≈595 where it meets the fog coat, so I need to repaint its right half so the dome completes naturally instead of cutting off hard. The peachy glow along the horizon behind the butte looks fine as is.

Looking closer at that hard edge, I realize the fog coat's smoothstep mask should fade smoothly from x=590 to 665, but the paint still shows a near-vertical cliff right around x=595-600 even though the mask value there should be nearly zero — so my assumption that stroke opacity scales continuously with mask value must be wrong, and instead there's likely a threshold effect anchoring strokes wherever the mask crosses some cutoff.

So it seems soft masks alone don't create soft edges in this system; I need the dedicated `edge` parameter (crisp to lost) to actually dissolve the boundary, and I should test that on a small patch before applying it to the full fog coat.

What I really want at the hill B / fog junction is for the gray hill's lower flank to fade gradually into the fog rather than hitting a hard edge, which likely means repainting hill B's dome and flank so the fog veils it with a soft diagonal gradient instead of relying on the mask trick.

I'm settling on a sequence: finish the butte body and talus now, then lay a second fog bank with a soft blended edge, then redraw hump B's full dome across its span with the tree line opaque on top, and finally add a third fog layer blended over the hill's base to achieve that fade.

Since calls are the real cost, I'm weighing painting butte and hills wet-in-wet together versus spacing them with drying waits to avoid unwanted mixing where they overlap near the talus.

Actually, unlike the sky where paints don't overlap, here fog glazed over wet rock would grey and pull up the darker paint, so I shouldn't do it wet-in-wet. I'll go step by step, starting with defining the butte's silhouette more precisely, flaring its base into talus and reconsidering its scale for focal weight.

The needle, tower, and step are already painted and dry as separate pieces sitting on the sky, so I just need to repaint the body below the plateau and extend it downward while keeping the dry top elements and their vertical cliff edges consistent.

I want to soften the talus skirt I sketched earlier — making it curve out concave rather than trapezoid-straight, with a ragged wavy outline from trees, and blending the cliff-to-talus transition with dark tree dabs overlapping the lower rock edges. Now I'm writing the hand-drawn outline polygon for the combined butte and talus body.

I want the cliff to be a cool lilac fading to warmth on the left down to around y≈430, then the forested talus taking over below that and dissolving into fog by y≈480 — rendered as stippled, dabbed texture rather than a smooth gradient so it reads organically. My earlier attempt using a hard polygon mask with filbert dabs produced a mottled lattice-like cell pattern instead of a convincing dark forest, so I need to rethink the color mix and coverage to avoid that artifact.

I realize the paint came out too light and thin — mixing smalt, raw umber, Prussian blue, white, and red earth gave a pale blue-gray wash over the fog base instead of a dark canopy. I need to cut the white, thicken the application, and build the forest from a darker pile (raw umber, Prussian blue, bone black, green earth) with just a touch of smalt/white for coolness, letting it lighten toward the bottom where it meets the fog — or alternatively, skip the forested talus entirely and let the cliff base dissolve straight into soft fog.

Going with the cleaner approach — rock rising from fog, cliff as a visible vertical mass with the fog bank hiding the base around y≈445. To avoid a "bucket in fog" look, I'll give the outline irregular notches and buttresses, plus a modest talus flare of about 20 units on each side between y 415–450, dotted with dark tree dabs and softly veiled by the fog below y=445. Now I'm thinking through how to handle the plateau top.

For the cliff faces, instead of a smooth vertical gradient (which reads as a cylinder), I want to break it into several faceted vertical slabs — alternating lighter warm tones and darker cool tones, like 4-5 buttress planes with an arete around x≈795, to give it a more natural sandstone-tower feel.

Continuing the remaining slabs with the left-to-right darkening scheme, with light raking from the low sun on the left catching each pillar's left edge while shading its right side, applying vertical strokes and a gentle blend across the whole cliff face.

Writing body polygon coordinates...

I need to match left and right silhouettes to the old edges near the top so there's no visible seam, keeping x=745 for the left edge and x=870 for the right at the transition height. Then I'm setting up the slab painting pass using the existing color piles with a filbert brush, vertical strokes, and clipped fill for each slab polygon.

For softening the boundaries, I realize a vertical blend would just smear paint along the slab edges rather than softening them — I actually need a horizontal blend to blur across the vertical cliffs, followed by a light vertical blend to keep things natural. That combination should be quick enough to not add much overhead.

For the tree-line at the cliff's foot, I'm planning a ragged band of dark filbert dabs around y 425–445, mostly vertical orientation with varied lengths, then fogging over the lower portion with a soft edge. After that dries, I'll add a second fog bank near the butte whose top edge rises toward the ridges on either side, layered over the first dry fog coat.

Since the butte's base needs coverage from y≈448 to 490 with the same pigment blending into the existing fog on both sides, edge transitions will only be visible against the butte itself. Time to start painting the butte body now.

ScMid   = pile{{"raw umber",1.4},{"Prussian blue",0.3},{"smalt",1.5},{"green earth",0.3},{"lead white",1.1},{"red earth",0.2}}
ScFar   = pile{{"lead white",2.3},{"smalt",2.0},{"raw umber",0.45},{"red earth",0.3},{"Prussian blue",0.06}}

dab = {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", angle=1.35, coverage=5.0, clip=true, fill=true, length={5,14}, angle_jitter=0.6}
function dabwork(m, p, cov, tool, extra)
  local o = {hand="body", tool=tool or "filbert 8", pile=p, angle=1.35, coverage=cov, clip=true, fill=true, length={5,14}, angle_jitter=0.6}
  if extra then for k, v in pairs(extra) do o[k] = v end end
  work(m, o)
end

I'll keep the main silhouette mostly intact to avoid redoing the sky, but add small projecting buttresses and a pinnacle to make the edges feel more natural, while reworking the awkward needle, dome, and step shapes into believable sandstone rock formations in the same dark-blue tone.

The cliff's turned into a flat gray-lilac blob now, having lost its warm light and form after the blending overwrote the lit band — it reads like a bulbous gray cake. I need to let it dry and then add fine strokes to rebuild surface detail, and really rethink the whole approach to make this feel like a convincing sandstone butte.

What makes rock read as rock: sharp value contrast between lit and shadow planes along vertical arêtes, dark fissures and horizontal ledges, overhanging cornices with shadows beneath, tiny clinging trees on ledges, and rough stippled texture. I'm thinking of building the surface as vertical pillar-like slabs with varying values, similar to an earlier attempt that got blended away but had a decent fluted look before — though it still ended up reading as bucket-shaped. As an alternative, I'm considering constructing the butte as a proper 3D form using lighting and value functions to compute shading from a single light source across the solid shape.

I could build a rock mass from a rough, perturbed block, then derive lit and shadow masks from its geometry to paint warm into lit areas and cool into shadow, giving coherent geometry-based lighting for both the butte and the trunk. The silhouette would come from the solid itself, built as a union of several rough pillars of varying height and depth so the lighting naturally breaks into planes, with the lit/shadow masks intersected against the existing cliff mask to stay within the painted area.

Actually, rather than building actual solids, it's simpler to just manually paint each pillar with its own gradient -- warm light fading to dark across its width -- with dark gaps between them to create that "organ pipe" rhythm across roughly eight pillars.

I'm planning uneven pillar boundaries across the cliff, with the left-side pillars getting brighter, warmer light (since the glow source sits to the left) and the right-side ones fading into shadow and coolness, each pillar lit on its left edge and shadowed on its right.

Layering masked gradients per pillar...

Then I'll add post-drying fissures as thin dark wobbly lines at pillar boundaries with partial lengths, and confirm the layered veil approach reads correctly since lower-load layers still leave a faint transparent tint over the darker base, consistent with the intended gradient effect.

Since the cliff is now a uniform gray, painting over wet is fine, so I'll move on to the pillars with moderate coverage. Then I should reconsider the top of the composition — maybe a crown of forest there.

function spruce(x, yb, h, w, lean, pile_)

The spruce reads too much like a stiff Christmas tree — the branches are too thin and sparse, giving it a pylon-like silhouette instead of a dense, layered mass. I need thicker, darker strokes with ragged edges to create that narrow conical but bough-heavy profile real spruces have at this scale.

Working out the sawtooth path: each bough droops down to its tip, then the outline cuts back inward and upward to the next notch higher up before heading out to the following tip, so I need notch heights lower than the previous tip to get that hanging-bough look.

Once the outline's set, I'll fill the polygon with interior detail strokes and layer fringe strokes on top for texture, then vary tier count, height, and shape randomly across trees.

function spruceMask(x, yb, h, w, lean)
  lean = lean or 0
  local ytop = yb - h
  local n = math.max(8, math.floor(h/4.2))
  local s = h / n
  local function tx(y) return x + lean*(yb - y) end
  local left, right = {}, {}
  left[#left+1] = {tx(ytop), ytop - 1}
  for i = 1, n do
    local t = i / n
    local yn = ytop + s*(i-1) + s*0.25
    local L = (w/2) * (0.10 + 0.90*t^0.85)
    local xn = tx(yn) - L*0.38*rand(0.8,1.2)
    local yt = yn + s*rand(1.3, 1.8)
    local xt = tx(yt) - L*rand(0.85, 1.12)
    left[#left+1] = {xn, yn}
    left[#left+1] = {xt, yt}
  end
  right[#right+1] = {tx(ytop), ytop - 1}
  for i = 1, n do
    local t = i / n
    local yn = ytop + s*(i-1) + s*0.25
    local L = (w/2) * (0.10 + 0.90*t^0.85)
    local xn = tx(yn) + L*0.38*rand(0.8,1.2)
    local yt = yn + s*rand(1.3, 1.8)
    local xt = tx(yt) + L*rand(0.85, 1.12)
    right[#right+1] = {xn, yn}
    right[#right+1] = {xt, yt}
  end
  local p = {}
  for _, q in ipairs(left) do p[#p+1] = q end
  -- base across the bottom
  p[#p+1] = {left[#left][1] + 3, yb + 1.5}
  p[#p+1] = {right[#right][1] - 3, yb + 1.5}
  for i = #right, 1, -1 do p[#p+1] = right[i] end
  return poly(p)
end
function spruceFull(x, yb, h, w, lean, pile_)
  local m = spruceMask(x, yb, h, w, lean)
  work(m, {hand="detail", pile=pile_, coverage=4.0, clip=true, angle=1.5708, length={3,8}, pressure={0.5,0.9}})
  -- the trunk and leader
  spB:load(pile_, 1.0)
  spB:stroke({{x, yb+1.5}, {x + lean*h*0.4, yb - h*0.45}, {x + lean*h, yb - h - 3}}, {pressure={0.55, 0.15}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  -- hanging fringe along the outer tips (thin dark strokes drooping from the tier ends)
  local ytop = yb - h
  local n = math.max(8, math.floor(h/4.2))
  local s = h / n
  for i = 2, n do
    local t = i / n
    local y = ytop + s*(i-1) + s*1.4
    local L = (w/2) * (0.10 + 0.90*t^0.85)
    for _, sd in ipairs({-1, 1}) do
      local fx = x + lean*(yb - y) + sd*L*rand(0.7, 1.1)
      spB:load(pile_, 0.7)
      spB:stroke({{fx, y - s*0.4}, {fx + sd*s*0.2, y + s*0.4}, {fx + sd*s*0.4, y + s*1.1}}, {pressure={0.42, 0.1}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
    end
  end
end

function joint(x0, y0, y1, w, wob, seed)
  local pts, ws = {}, {}
  local n = math.max(3, math.floor((y1-y0)/9))
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    pts[#pts+1] = {x0 + wob*math.sin(i*1.9 + seed) + rand(-0.5,0.5), y0 + (y1-y0)*t}
    ws[#ws+1] = w*(0.6 + 0.7*math.sin(3.14*t)) 
  end
  return ribbon(pts, ws)
end

function lit_blade(bx, by, h, lean, pile_, wmax, load)
  local n = 5
  local pts = {}
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    local bend = lean * (0.25 + t*t*1.6)
    pts[#pts+1] = {bx + math.sin(bend) * h * t, by - math.cos(bend) * h * t}
  end

end

TWIGS = {}
-- re-define the shoot generators so every polyline is recorded
function oakshoot3(x, y, ang, len, w0, depth, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local pts = {{x, y}}
  local angs = {}
  local cx, cy, a = x, y, ang
  local used = 0
  local kink = opts.kink or 0.5
  while used < len do
    local l = math.min(rand(opts.lmin or 8, opts.lmax or 17), len - used)
    if l < 3.0 then break end
    a = a + rand(-kink, kink) - (opts.up or 0.04) * math.sin(a)
    cx = cx + math.cos(a) * l
    cy = cy + math.sin(a) * l
    used = used + l
    pts[#pts+1] = {cx, cy}
    angs[#angs+1] = a
  end
  if #pts < 2 then return end
  local w1 = math.max(0.87, w0 * 0.3)
  tw:load(OakT, 1.0)
  tw:stroke(pts, {pressure={tw:pressure_for(math.max(w0, 0.9)), tw:pressure_for(w1)}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  TWIGS[#TWIGS+1] = pts
  if depth > 0 then
    local total = used
    local d = 0
    for i = 2, #pts do
      d = d + math.sqrt((pts[i][1]-pts[i-1][1])^2 + (pts[i][2]-pts[i-1][2])^2)
      if math.random() < (opts.p or 0.6) then
        local side = (math.random() < 0.5) and 1 or -1
        local sa = angs[i-1] + side * rand(0.4, 0.95)
        local rem = total - d
        local sl = math.max(7, (rem + rand(5, 16)) * rand(0.45, 0.85))
        oakshoot3(pts[i][1], pts[i][2], sa, sl, math.max(0.9, w0 * 0.75), depth - 1, opts)
      end
    end
  end
end
function sprout4(name, from, to, spacing, wcap, depth, lenmin, lenmax, opts)
  local L = OAK[name]
  local pts, wd = L[1], L[2]
  local s = {0}
  for i = 2, #pts do
    s[i] = s[i-1] + math.sqrt((pts[i][1]-pts[i-1][1])^2 + (pts[i][2]-pts[i-1][2])^2)
  end
  local total = s[#pts]
  local pos = total * from
  local flip = (math.random() < 0.5) and 1 or -1
  while pos < total * to do
    local i = 1
    while i < #pts-1 and s[i+1] < pos do i = i + 1 end
    local t = (pos - s[i]) / (s[i+1] - s[i])
    local px = pts[i][1] + t * (pts[i+1][1]-pts[i][1])
    local py = pts[i][2] + t * (pts[i+1][2]-pts[i][2])
    local la = math.atan(pts[i+1][2]-pts[i][2], pts[i+1][1]-pts[i][1])
    local wl = wd[i] + t * (wd[i+1]-wd[i])
    local sa = la + flip * rand(0.35, 0.85)
    flip = -flip
    oakshoot3(px, py, sa, rand(lenmin, lenmax), clamp(wl * 0.42, 0.9, wcap), depth, opts)
    pos = pos + spacing * rand(0.7, 1.3)
  end
  -- terminal fan at the limb's tip
  local n = #pts
  local la = math.atan(pts[n][2]-pts[n-1][2], pts[n][1]-pts[n-1][1])
  for k = 1, 3 do
    oakshoot3(pts[n][1], pts[n][2], la + (k-2) * rand(0.3, 0.55), rand(lenmin*0.8, lenmax), clamp(wd[n]*0.9, 0.9, wcap), depth, opts)
  end
end
-- first generation: from the big limbs
for _, nm in ipairs({"L2","L1","L4","L5"}) do
  sprout4(nm, 0.45, 1.0, 17, 3.2, 2, 34, 66, {p=0.6})
end
for _, nm in ipairs({"R1","R1a","R1b"}) do
  sprout4(nm, 0.45, 1.0, 17, 3.4, 2, 34, 70, {p=0.6})
end

The right half is messy with a flat cream background and a floating butte with a hard rectangular base, while the left oak side is solid. I want to fix the right half efficiently, keeping in mind that clipping produces crisp boundaries matching the mask exactly.

My plan is to do a single wet-in-wet pass over the entire right valley region, blending broad strokes together and painting the forest at the butte's foot directly into the still-wet fog so it dissolves naturally — since a dark stroke dragged through wet pale paint will come out grayed and hazy, which actually works in my favor here, making the forest merge softly into the mist.

Alternatively, I could let the fog dry first, then stipple the forest's edge with feathered density so each touch stays distinct, and finish with a lost-edge glaze — this dry approach gives more control than the wet blend did for the butte's crisp dab-work edges. I'm leaning toward the dry stipple method, but I also need to fix a visible seam where the new cream fog meets the older lilac fog along a vertical line — probably best solved with a scumbled, feathered dab across the boundary since the paint is already dry.

I want to be careful not to disturb the left side of the fog sea, where the layered lilac hills and ridges behind the oak already read well. For the right side, I'm picturing Friedrich's "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog" — a soft, nearly uniform cream-gray-blue expanse with gentle swells, rocks breaking the surface, and faint mountains dissolving into the brightened horizon.

Right now the fog there reads too uniformly bright, almost whiter than the peach sky at the horizon, which feels off given the afterglow behind it. I want to rework it into a luminous pale lilac-pink-cream that sits just under the horizon's brightness, then cools and darkens toward the foreground, built up in soft tonal bands from the warm horizon down to the cooler near fog.

I also need to handle the fog meeting the cliff's forested foot — the cream mist should wrap the lower part of the forest with wisps crossing the dark trees, but right now the coat has covered too much of that transition cleanly instead of leaving a soft, misty edge.

Rebuilding the butte's foot as a proper widening talus slope that dissolves into fog is the fix for the floating problem — I'll give it an organic base spreading outward on both sides rather than the current rectangular cliff edge, with fog bands crossing in front at different heights to ground it.

A brushed glaze isn't clipped, so its edges extend past the mask by the stroke length under light pressure, with mask value just anchoring where strokes start; using load_at for variation gives thin, smooth films for tonal gradation, confirming glazes work well there while opaque coats are reserved for resetting colour.

Right now I need an opaque flat cream base first, then glaze gradation over it — a cool lilac transparent mix over the cream for the bottom, warm peach near the horizon, which I've done successfully before. But the seam at x=606 is a hard hue/value step, so a glaze alone won't erase it; I'll likely need to repaint the left side of the seam directly with a wet-in-wet scumble.

Looking at the crop, the seam runs from y≈410–560 and is quite visible — old lilac-gray misty structure on the left versus flat cream on the right. A better fix might be extending the new fog coat leftward across x~290–606 to unify the whole valley behind the oak's limbs and the figure, since the figure needs to read clearly against pale fog rather than the lilac hill currently behind him.

I need to avoid painting over the oak's twig network there, so I'm considering building a mask from the recorded twig polylines — but with 1360 polylines, generating a full ribbon mask for each and summing them would be memory-heavy and slow, even if temporary. I'm weighing whether a single combined ribbon function or a different masking approach would be more efficient.

Evaluating a per-pixel distance function to the nearest twig segment would be too slow across 4 million pixels, so instead I'm leaning toward precomputing a coarse low-resolution grid in Lua — marking cells within a small radius of each twig segment — so the mask lookup becomes a fast grid query rather than a live distance calculation.

This mask protects my own painted twig marks, which seems legitimate rather than encoding an external image. Though I'm now considering whether a fog coat with a hole around each twig would leave a visible halo of old lilac-colored paint showing through near the twigs.

To avoid this ghosting effect, I should exclude only the twig's exact footprint with a tight radius rather than a wide buffer, so the cream coat comes right up to the twig edges without leaving a visible fringe. Alternatively, I could simply repaint the twigs afterward since their polylines are recorded and can be re-stroked with the same brush.

Actually, do I even need full re-stroking? The left fog region near the trunk already shows lilac hills giving natural depth, so the seam issue is really just localized at x=606. A better fix might be to feather the new cream coat's edge into the old lilac-gray fog across x=540–640 with a density-dissolve stipple instead of redoing all the twigs.

I need to check this stipple zone against L4's drooping limb tip, which reaches into that same region around x 480–585, y 425–500 — so I'd need to clip the feathering around a small rectangle excluding the L4 tip area to avoid overlapping its twigs.

Actually, simpler might be to let the scumble lay down first and then re-stroke any twigs whose points fall in that rect afterward, pulling from the full twig polyline list and redrawing with the same oak-bark brush. That seems workable, though I'm also weighing whether to just soften the fog coat on the right half instead of fussing with the seam boundary directly.

Stepping back, I want to prioritize what actually matters for a convincing Friedrich-style composition: the oak silhouette and sky are solid, the figure is small but fine, the foreground crest works though it could use more texture variation like rocks or darker tufts, and the right valley's fog sea is the remaining piece to nail down.

That valley takes up nearly half the canvas, so it needs real care — layered fog, a butte rising through it, distant ridges with soft atmospheric color, maybe a second peak far off. Right now it's just flat cream, so I'm weighing whether to rebuild it fresh with broad wet-in-wet bands like I did for the sky, versus working with the dried layer already there.

Since the cream might still be workable, I could glaze over it instead: a cool lilac-gray wash that intensifies toward the bottom and right, a warm peach glow near the horizon, then soft swell shapes, followed by a stippled butte base and final wisps. I'm also thinking about how to blend the seam between old and new paint using feathered stippling and a unifying lilac glaze.

The lilac barely registers against the cream since the pigment ratios are too close to the previous mix. I need to push it deeper with more smalt and red earth, then paint a wet-in-wet band transitioning from cream at the top into lilac around y=560 and a deeper blue-gray lilac at the crest near y=640.

Now for the seam at x=606 — the left side is already dry from an earlier pass, so new wet strokes there won't blend in the same way; they'll sit as a fresh coat on top. To avoid a visible hard edge where the new wet paint meets the old dry paint, I should feather that boundary with a lost edge so the transition reads as seamless.

I also need to revisit the cliff — the rectangle exclusion left the lower section mostly bare except for the forest strip, so I'll rebuild that foot once everything dries. The sensible order is: do the wet-in-wet fog modulations on the right now with the lost left edge, let it dry, then come back for the butte foot, swells, and wisps.

But another option is covering the old lilac fog entirely between the trunk and seam, carving around the figure and branches — though that feels heavier than just letting the edge dissolve into the existing cream, which is still wet and simpler to work with. Still, I'm unsure what that old lilac fog region with its dome details actually looks like now, so I need to check the full view before committing.

Looking again, I realize that vertical seam against the cream could actually work as a mist bank if I make the boundary wavy and irregular instead of straight — a soft, drifting edge reads naturally as fog in front of the hill, so I'll paint a new lost edge whose boundary meanders between roughly x=560 and 650 rather than trying to erase the existing structure.

Stippling on dry layers could give a lacy, dotty texture fine for mist, unified with a final glaze -- but a glaze reduces contrast only slightly, not the underlying value gap. I think I should just examine the actual seam region in its current state before deciding how to proceed.

I'm checking the seam around x=606, where the horizon now shows a clean edge between the peach sky and cream fog, and the cream coat has covered the old ridge band. To the left, the lilac-gray mountain slope and fog blend reasonably well.

There's a visible edge where the lilac hill abruptly meets the cream fog, especially in the lower section. I want to extend the hill's slope further right with a feathered, ragged edge so it dissolves gradually into the fog rather than stopping sharply, creating a smoother hill-to-fog-to-rock transition.

Thinking more broadly, I realize the whole right valley needs a layered second pass: restoring the far horizon ridge (a pale lilac strip that's been buried under the fog coat), including the faint remnant visible at the top right near the butte, and rebuilding it systematically layer by layer starting with that distant ridge band.

I want to simplify dramatically, following Friedrich's example of a fog sea dominated by mist with just a few rock peaks poking through, rather than trying to recreate every hump and dome from before. My plan is to build it wet-in-wet, top to bottom, letting each layer blend into the next while still wet.

I'm extending the fog mask leftward with a soft lost edge, and deciding to paint the foot forest directly into the wet fog near the cliff base so the blender can soften that transition too. I'm sketching out a single session plan, maybe 1-2 hours of active painting with roughly 2-3 hours of workable wet time overall.

Actually simpler to skip the left extension and instead shape the new fog's left edge as a wavy, drifting boundary that sits entirely left of the old seam at x=606, so the fresh paint fully covers the previous cream edge across the 410–560 vertical range, letting the lost-edge dissolve blend naturally.

Choosing a wavy left boundary further out (around 596±12) with a 15-20 unit feathered dissolve avoids conflict with L4's twigs entirely since they end near x=585. I'll keep the lost-edge effect limited to just that left boundary, leaving the crest line and cliff edges crisp, and treat this as a test render to check before committing further.

A crisp horizon between peach sky and cream fog feels too harsh, so I'm thinking of softening it with a lilac ridge strip that dissolves into the fog below through wet-in-wet blending. I want to keep this simple rather than over-engineer it, so I'm starting to define the fog region, excluding the cliff area from the mask.

Defining a new masked region that bounds the fog by the ridge's upper edge and the horizon line, then subtracting the cliff shape and sprites from it, accounting for the cliff's straight bottom edge at the forest foot...

Next I'm laying the fog base coat over Rv to blend the seam, then painting the ridge strip with a graded lilac load that's strong at top and fades downward, using a soft lost edge at the lower mask boundary so it dissolves into the following fog layer rather than leaving a crisp line.

Then I'll replicate that approach for the A2R humps, add a deeper lilac lower fog band and a cream mid band with lost top edges, and dab in the butte foot forest with density fading by height. I'm also considering whether to just apply a universal "lost" edge setting across all these layers instead of customizing each one.

Beyond edges, I need to work out the fog's color relationship to the sky: near the horizon it should echo the peach-yellow glow at its brightest point, then shift progressively cooler, paler, and slightly darker as it descends toward the viewer, with the sun-glow potentially backlighting it.

I'm mixing pigment ratios for a family of fog tones — cool and warm creams, peach cream, and several lilac-grays of increasing saturation — to give myself a gradient palette to work from.

I'm also working out the value hierarchy from lightest to darkest across the scene, and considering adding a second, fainter distant peak to the right of the butte for atmospheric depth, echoing Friedrich's layered mountain compositions.

The hard rectangular silhouette with its straight vertical sides and flat bottom feels too pasted-on, so I want to roughen the edges, add stepped ledges, and darken the shadow side before the fog dissolves the base anyway. Since the cream layer is still wet and it's day 276, 09:22, now's the time to do the wet-in-wet session.

I'm defining a region mask with a wavy left edge function and setting up a lost-edge coverage stroke over the seam, letting it overrun into the old lilac strip to blend naturally — mindful that each stroke eats time and I only have a couple hours before the paint sets.

These speckled crowns are reading as dark cartoonish blobs rather than a believable forest, so I need to rethink the butte's base. I want it to feel like a solid, softly modeled forested slope rising into fog, built from dabs of mid blue-green tones with subtle lighting rather than noisy speckles.

After the current coat dries, I'll paint the forest as one cohesive wet-in-wet mass—a rounded mound with an irregular, tree-like top edge where the cliff paint comes down in jagged "fingers." Then once dry, I'll lay a thin cream fog glaze over the lower portion, graded so the color fades to nothing smoothly; since the glaze is so thin, it should blend seamlessly into the surrounding mist without leaving a visible hard edge.

I'd apply the glaze over a wide region using a smooth gradient in both x and y, extending the mask beyond the forest mass to cover part of the cliff base (good for a hazy effect) while leaving the fog unchanged since it's already the same cream tone. The stipple dots now sitting in the wet fog are a problem, but rather than smearing them by painting over while still wet, I'll wait until dry and recoat with fresh cream in a mask that spares the cliff.

So the plan becomes: wait about nine days for it to dry, then lay a cream coat over the mound area (invisible against the surrounding fog since it's the same color), paint the forest mass, then glaze — rejecting the idea of keeping the speckled look since it reads as noise rather than Friedrich-style atmosphere. While waiting, I can use the time on other dry areas like the oak's rim lights, sky clouds, birds, or the foreground.

Since the sky is already dry, now I'll design the stratus cloud bands — a few thin, slanted bars in the upper-middle sky to the right of the oak, cool grey-lilac on top with warm pink undersides lit by the afterglow, positioning two long bands at different heights across the sky.

I want these to avoid the lens-shaped, sharp-edged "pill" look from before by using soft-edged, streaky strokes with noisy elongated blob masks for irregular, broken banding, dragged in a near-horizontal direction with low coverage.

Weighing it though, the current sky already reads nicely as a clear dusk gradient with just a faint trace near (490, 65), and Friedrich himself painted plenty of clear, cloudless skies—so maybe leaving it alone is the safer, more elegant choice rather than risking a poorly executed cloud.

That said, a couple of faint stratus streaks near the horizon right of the butte might help tie the glow into the ridge. But really, the valley and butte are the weaker areas and deserve more attention. While the fog dries, I can turn to other non-conflicting work: the buried spruces at lower right need to wait until the fog sets, the left seam should be dry by now, and the foreground below y>600 is ready for a unifying glaze.

Let me zoom into the bottom region at 1:1 before deciding how to proceed.

The foreground is a plain dark brown with blocky patches that could use unifying — the dark simplicity fits a Friedrich painting, but a lighter rectangular patch at the right edge stands out distractingly. function segDist2(px, py, s)
  local dx, dy = s[3]-s[1], s[4]-s[2]
  local l2 = dx*dx + dy*dy
  local t = 0
  if l2 > 0 then t = clamp(((px-s[1])*dx + (py-s[2])*dy)/l2, 0, 1) end
  local qx, qy = s[1]+t*dx, s[2]+t*dy
  return (px-qx)^2 + (py-qy)^2
end

  for i = 1, #segs do

  end
  return 0

Fc = function(x) return 424 + 6*math.sin(x/13 + 0.5) + 3*math.sin(x/5.3) end
xb2 = function(y) return 556 + 10*math.sin(y/29) + 6*math.sin(y/11 + 1) end

segs2 = {}
for _, pts in ipairs(TWIGS) do

    if math.max(a[1], b[1]) > 440 and math.min(a[1], b[1]) < 680 and math.max(a[2], b[2]) > 350 and math.min(a[2], b[2]) < 570 then

  if x < 440 or x > 680 or y < 350 or y > 570 then return 0 end
  for i = 1, #segs2 do

gidx = {}

-- ===== hazy wooded hills rising out of the fog (right half) =====
clipH = (rect(540, 396, 480, 230) - guardT - fgM - cliffM:grow(1.0)) - spr1 - spr2m - spr3
function softHill(pts, amp, seed, x0, x1, depth, pile_, cov, tool_, fadeEnds)
  local topf = function(x) return interp(pts, x) + amp*trn(x*1.0 + seed, 3.0) end
  local m = mask(function(x,y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local t = topf(x)
    return smoothstep(t-0.6, t+0.6, y) * ((y < t + depth) and 1 or 0)
  end)
  local edgeFn = function(x,y)
    local t = topf(x)
    local bottom = smoothstep(t + depth*0.30, t + depth*0.9, y)
    local ends = 0
    if fadeEnds then
      ends = math.max(1 - smoothstep(x0, x0 + 80, x), smoothstep(x1 - 80, x1, x))
    end
    return clamp(math.max(0.05 + 0.9*bottom, 0.9*ends), 0, 1)
  end
  work(m, {hand="body", tool=tool_ or "filbert 12", pile=pile_, angle=0.03, coverage=cov or 4.0, fill=true, length={30,90}, angle_jitter=0.15,
    clip=clipH, edge=edgeFn})
  return m
end

clipH2 = (rect(596, 440, 420, 240) - guardT - fgM - cliffM:grow(1.0))
function softHill2(pts, amp, seed, x0, x1, depth, pile_, cov, tool_, bottomLost)
  local topf = function(x) return interp(pts, x) + amp*trn(x*1.0 + seed, 3.0) end
  local m = mask(function(x,y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local t = topf(x)
    return smoothstep(t-0.6, t+0.6, y) * ((y < t + depth) and 1 or 0)
  end) * clipH2
  local edgeFn = function(x,y)
    local t = topf(x)
    local bottom = smoothstep(t + depth*0.20, t + depth*0.85, y)
    local ends = math.max(1 - smoothstep(x0, x0 + 70, x), smoothstep(x1 - 70, x1, x))
    return clamp(math.max(0.04 + 0.92*bottom, 0.95*ends), 0, 1)
  end
  work(m, {hand="body", tool=tool_ or "filbert 12", pile=pile_, angle=0.03, coverage=cov or 4.0, fill=true, length={30,90}, angle_jitter=0.15,
    clip=clipH2, edge=edgeFn,
    load_at=function(x,y) local t = topf(x); return clamp(1.0 - 0.55*smoothstep(t+depth*0.3, t+depth, y), 0.2, 1) end})
  return m
end
