-- ===== hills in the fog, by paint-merging (the mask boundary vanishes because paint == fog there) =====
hillRock = {["lead white"]=2.4, ["smalt"]=2.0, ["raw umber"]=0.45, ["red earth"]=0.3, ["Prussian blue"]=0.06}
hillNear = {["smalt"]=1.6, ["raw umber"]=0.7, ["lead white"]=1.6, ["red earth"]=0.3, ["green earth"]=0.25, ["Prussian blue"]=0.15}
fogTab = {["lead white"]=7, ["pale smalt"]=0.6, ["red earth"]=0.12, ["yellow ochre"]=0.12}
fracs = {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}
function fogHill(pts, amp, seed, x0, x1, depth, rockT, fadeAt, tool_)
  local topf = function(x) return interp(pts, x) + amp*trn(x*1.0 + seed, 3.0) end
  local ext = 46   -- the mask runs well past the visible hill; there the paint is pure fog
  local M = mask(function(x,y)
    if x < x0 - ext or x > x1 + ext then return 0 end
    local t = topf(math.max(x0, math.min(x1, x)))
    -- ends: the top profile continues down into the fog so no step shows
    local endDrop = 0
    if x < x0 then endDrop = (x0 - x) * 1.1 elseif x > x1 then endDrop = (x - x1) * 1.1 end
    local tt = t + endDrop
    return smoothstep(tt-0.6, tt+0.6, y) * ((y < t + depth) and 1 or 0)
  end) * (rect(560, 430, 460, 260) - guardT - fgM - cliffM:grow(1.0))
  local fy = function(x,y)
    local t = topf(math.max(x0, math.min(x1, x)))
    return smoothstep(t + depth*0.10, t + depth*fadeAt, y)
  end
  local fxf = function(x)
    return math.max(1 - smoothstep(x0, x0 + 60, x), smoothstep(x1 - 60, x1, x))
  end
  local F = function(x,y) return clamp(math.max(fy(x,y), fxf(x)), 0, 1) end
  for k, fr_ in ipairs(fracs) do
    local p = mixp(rockT, fogTab, fr_)
    local w = function(x,y)
      local f = F(x,y)
      return clamp(1 - math.abs(f - fr_)/0.26, 0, 1)
    end
    work(M, {hand="body", tool=tool_ or "filbert 9", pile=p, angle=0.02, coverage=4.0, clip=true, fill=true, length={14,50}, angle_jitter=0.15,
      load_at=w})
  end
  blend(M, {angle=0.0})
  return M
end

CbodyQ = pile{{"lead white",5.2},{"smalt",1.3},{"red earth",0.3},{"raw umber",0.12},{"yellow ochre",0.05}, medium=0.45}

function streak(xa, ya, xb, yb, wmul, p1, p2)
  local n = 6
  local pts = {}
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    pts[#pts+1] = {xa + (xb-xa)*t, ya + (yb-ya)*t + rand(-0.9, 0.9)}
  end
  cb1:load(CbodyQ, p1 or 0.85)
  cb1:stroke(pts, {pressure={0.5*(wmul or 1), 0.12}, ramps={0.12, 0.0}, clip=cloudClip})
  -- the warm lower lip, thin and shorter, a hair below
  local pts2 = {}
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    pts2[#pts2+1] = {xa + (xb-xa)*(0.1 + 0.8*t), ya + (yb-ya)*(0.1+0.8*t) + 3.2 + rand(-0.4, 0.4)}
  end
  cb2:load(CunderQ, p2 or 0.7)
  cb2:stroke(pts2, {pressure={0.4, 0.1}, ramps={0.15, 0.0}, clip=cloudClip})
end

pineD2 = pile{{"raw umber",1.4},{"bone black",0.9},{"green earth",0.45},{"Prussian blue",0.18}}
function spruceRag(x, yb, h, w, lean, pile_, density)
  lean = lean or 0
  local ytop = yb - h
  local N = math.floor(h * (density or 0.9))
  for k = 1, N do
    local t = rand(0.04, 0.99)^0.8            -- fraction down from the top; denser lower
    local y = ytop + h * t
    local tx = x + lean*h*(1 - t)
    local Lmax = (w/2) * (0.12 + 0.88*t^0.85)
    local side = (math.random() < 0.5) and -1 or 1
    local L = Lmax * rand(0.75, 1.45)
    local droop = L * rand(0.35, 0.95)
    local pts = {{tx, y}, {tx + side*L*0.4, y + droop*0.1}, {tx + side*L*0.75, y + droop*0.45}, {tx + side*L, y + droop}}
    spB:load(pile_, 0.9)
    spB:stroke(pts, {pressure={0.5, 0.1}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
    -- hanging fringe from the outer half of the bough
    local nf = math.random(1, 3)
    for j = 1, nf do
      local u = rand(0.45, 1.0)
      local fx = tx + side*L*u
      local fy = y + droop*(u^1.3)
      local fl = rand(0.12, 0.34) * L + 2
      spB:load(pile_, 0.8)
      spB:stroke({{fx, fy}, {fx + side*fl*0.12, fy + fl*0.55}, {fx + side*fl*0.2, fy + fl}}, {pressure={0.36, 0.08}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
    end
  end
  -- a ragged leader
  spB:load(pile_, 1.0)
  spB:stroke({{x + lean*h*0.97, ytop + 8}, {x + lean*h, ytop - 2}, {x + lean*h + rand(-0.8,0.8), ytop - 7}}, {pressure={0.4, 0.05}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
end
spruceRag(896, crestY(896)+3, 104, 46, 0.015, pineD2, 1.0)
spruceRag(951, crestY(951)+3, 70, 32, -0.02, pineD2, 1.0)
spruceRag(846, crestY(846)+3, 40, 20, 0.03, pineD2, 1.0)

ButBody  = {["smalt"]=1.2, ["raw umber"]=0.4, ["lead white"]=3.0, ["red earth"]=0.35, ["cobalt blue"]=0.15}

-- 2. shade on the right (irregular edge), 3. warm on the left

-- ===== exact guards: only the real twigs/limbs/figure are spared, no halos =====
GRID = 12
gidx = {}
local nseg = 0
for _, pts in ipairs(TWIGS) do
  for i = 1, #pts-1 do
    local a, b = pts[i], pts[i+1]
    if math.max(a[1], b[1]) > 270 and math.min(a[1], b[1]) < 720 and math.max(a[2], b[2]) > 330 and math.min(a[2], b[2]) < 590 then
      local s = {a[1], a[2], b[1], b[2]}
      nseg = nseg + 1
      local x0, x1 = math.floor((math.min(a[1], b[1]) - 4)/GRID), math.floor((math.max(a[1], b[1]) + 4)/GRID)
      local y0, y1 = math.floor((math.min(a[2], b[2]) - 4)/GRID), math.floor((math.max(a[2], b[2]) + 4)/GRID)
      for gx = x0, x1 do
        for gy = y0, y1 do
          local k = gx*1000 + gy
          local c = gidx[k]
          if not c then c = {}; gidx[k] = c end
          c[#c+1] = s
        end
      end
    end
  end
end
print("segments", nseg)
twigThin = mask(function(x, y)
  if x < 270 or x > 720 or y < 330 or y > 590 then return 0 end
  local c = gidx[math.floor(x/GRID)*1000 + math.floor(y/GRID)]
  if not c then return 0 end
  for i = 1, #c do
    if segDist2(x, y, c[i]) <= 2.4 then return 1 end
  end
  return 0
end)
guardX = limbsKeep:grow(0.4) + twigThin + figM:grow(1.2) + footM:grow(1.0)

The butte still reads as a pasted-on block, its lilac too close to the fog color but still looking like an odd hard-edged shape, and I notice a pale yellow halo ring around it left over from an earlier sky paint pass that excluded the butte zone with some buffer growth.

I need to repaint it entirely as a soft, convincing silhouette — a hazy blue-violet tabletop mountain, darker than the fog but lighter than the nearer hills, with a clean ridge line and its base dissolving into mist, thinking like Friedrich would: a quiet atmospheric shape with no texture, simple vertical planes with subtle value shifts. My earlier attempts using horizontal gradient bands came out streaky and crumpled-looking from the vertical blending strokes, so this time I'll try a smoother glaze approach with no medium blending to avoid that fluting texture.

The real problem is the dried, bumpy underlayers show through any glaze. I think the fix is to lay down a single opaque body coat with lead-white-rich, undiluted paint in one wet pass, blended wet-in-wet so the thick fluid paint levels out the raised ridges beneath it — then build the atmospheric gradient as a glaze on top once that's dry and smooth.

I recall trying something similar in "butte final" — the opaque body coat looked clean and pinkish-lilac, but the glaze I applied afterward left visible vertical streaks because I used vertical brush strokes on dried paint, leaving bristle marks instead of blending smoothly. So this time I want to work entirely wet-in-wet: lay the opaque color zones first with graduated hues, then glaze immediately while still wet so streaks blend out.

I'm also wondering whether the tree crowns from the earlier layer are still preserved under the new coat, since they were painted above the cliff top edge and might survive the re-coating process.

I could just expand the butte's growth mask to 2 units to overlap and cover that ring, which effectively enlarges the butte slightly but keeps the silhouette clean. Now I'm also reconsidering whether the pale-lilac butte shape itself is too wide and boxy, looking at the needle and tower forms again.

Overall it reads like a ghostly fortress on a cloud, which fits Friedrich's style, but it's too pale and the plateau top looks like a strange box. I think making the upper part a medium-dark blue-violet, fading lighter toward the base, would separate it better from the pale sky and give it more depth than its current washed-out value.

Writing the pigment mix definitions...

Looking more carefully, the butte's lower edge forms a hard horizontal line near y≈424, with the fog bank masking out the cliff foot below that and the wavy fog top sitting around y≈405–415. So I just need to paint the butte above that footline, letting the fog layer handle the transition beneath it.

Since the earlier coat is dry, a new opaque coat should cleanly cover it, and I still need to add the needle, tower, and step pieces. I also want to fix the pale ring issue by adjusting the coat mask to include those elements while excluding the small crown trees so they don't get painted over.

The trees were painted directly with ellipse and tiny pine masks rather than stored separately, so growing the mask by 1.8 would cover their lower trunks while leaving the tops visible, making them look like they're standing on the plateau — which seems acceptable, or I could re-add a few trees on top afterward.

I should wait until the butte coat dries before painting new trees on top, since wet-on-wet would dissolve them. As for the pale ring effect, growing the butte coat by 2.2 should cover it cleanly since the new darker blue-lilac coat will create a crisp silhouette over the lighter sky-glow ring. The picture is nearly complete now, so I'm pausing to evaluate the overall composition.

Going through each element: the sky gradient looks good with clouds confined to the right and a few faint streaks on the left; the oak's symmetrical crown with candelabra-like twigs reads well, though the trunk could use a touch more rim light; the figure is well-placed under the long limb; the dark foreground slope feels appropriately simple in Friedrich's style, if a bit plain; the lower-right spruces are fine; and I'm now looking at whether the fog sea reads smoothly.

I notice the pale lilac ridges behind the oak on the left side look a bit off — those grey-lilac masses have oddly straight diagonal edges that resemble snow slopes rather than natural hill humps, so I want to examine that area more closely. I'm also considering whether a thin warm glaze over the whole painting would help unify things, but that feels too risky and I'll skip it.

The left side behind the oak shows simple hazy ridge layers in lilac and grey-blue tones, with a ragged hilltop edge. I'm also spotting a jagged kink artifact in the lower-left limb that needs checking.

Turning to the butte's cliff face, I'm revisiting its polygon shape - needle at left, tower knob, and right step - and planning a three-zone coat: warm pinkish-grey on the lit left, cool lilac-blue mid-face, and darker blue-violet shading on the right, with soft boundaries that fade toward fog in the lower third. I want the top darker than the surrounding fog by a clear margin, roughly half-value, and I'm reconsidering the paint mixture ratios from the earlier butte body pass.

I'm setting new smalt-umber-white-earth-cobalt proportions for the cliff coat, computing the same band fraction structure but scaled to the cliff's actual foot line around y=424. I'll replicate the smooth blended approach from the earlier successful butte pass, but with slightly different colors and a wider mask to cover the ring, being careful to soften the seam where the cliff meets the fog zone below using some stippled dry-on-dry blending.

Now I'm building the combined mask from the cliff, needle, and tower shapes grown slightly and clipped to the foot line, then applying the shade/warm zone functions multiplied through that mask.

-- ===== the butte, once more: darker, bluer, soft; one opaque wet-in-wet session over the dry old coat =====
bNew = ((cliffM + needleM + towerK + step):grow(2.2)) * mask(function(x,y) return (y <= footLine(x) + 1.5) and 1 or 0 end)
print("bNew area", bNew:area())
NB = {}
NB.body  = {["smalt"]=1.7, ["raw umber"]=0.5, ["lead white"]=1.8, ["red earth"]=0.35, ["cobalt blue"]=0.2}
NB.shade = {["smalt"]=1.6, ["raw umber"]=0.85, ["lead white"]=1.0, ["red earth"]=0.3, ["Prussian blue"]=0.1}
NB.warm  = {["lead white"]=2.4, ["red earth"]=0.7, ["yellow ochre"]=0.5, ["smalt"]=0.45, ["vermilion"]=0.12}
nShade = bNew * mask(function(x,y) return smoothstep(shEdge(x,y)-12, shEdge(x,y)+12, x) end)
nWarm  = bNew * mask(function(x,y) return (1 - smoothstep(litEdge(x,y)-10, litEdge(x,y)+10, x)) end)
-- zero haze everywhere first: full-strength colours
work(bNew,   {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", pile=mixp(NB.body,  tFogC, 0.0), angle=0.0, coverage=6.0, clip=true, fill=true, length={8,22}, angle_jitter=0.08})
work(nShade, {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", pile=mixp(NB.shade, tFogC, 0.0), angle=0.0, coverage=4.0, clip=true, fill=true, length={8,22}, angle_jitter=0.08,
  load_at=function(x,y) return clamp(0.55 + 0.45*smoothstep(shEdge(x,y), 872, x), 0, 1) end})
work(nWarm,  {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", pile=mixp(NB.warm,  tFogW, 0.0), angle=0.0, coverage=4.0, clip=true, fill=true, length={8,22}, angle_jitter=0.08,
  load_at=function(x,y) return clamp(0.85*(1 - 0.5*smoothstep(345, 420, y)), 0, 1) end})
-- haze bands toward the foot
hb = {{0.18, 358, 392}, {0.40, 380, 410}, {0.62, 398, 421}, {0.82, 410, 430}}
for i, b in ipairs(hb) do
  local f, y0, y1 = b[1], b[2], b[3]
  local prof = function(y)
    local up = smoothstep(y0, y0 + 0.45*(y1-y0), y)
    local dn = (i == #hb) and 1 or (1 - smoothstep(y0 + 0.75*(y1-y0), y1, y))
    return clamp(up*dn, 0, 1)
  end
  local bm = rect(690, y0 - 2, 240, (y1 - y0) + 4)
  work(bNew * bm,   {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", pile=mixp(NB.body,  tFogC, f), angle=0.0, coverage=3.6, clip=true, fill=true, length={8,22}, angle_jitter=0.08, load_at=function(x,y) return prof(y) end})
  work(nShade * bm, {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", pile=mixp(NB.shade, tFogC, f), angle=0.0, coverage=3.2, clip=true, fill=true, length={8,22}, angle_jitter=0.08, load_at=function(x,y) return prof(y) end})
  work(nWarm * bm,  {hand="body", tool="filbert 8", pile=mixp(NB.warm,  tFogW, f), angle=0.0, coverage=3.2, clip=true, fill=true, length={8,22}, angle_jitter=0.08, load_at=function(x,y) return prof(y) end})
end

GRID2 = 12
gidx2 = {}
local nseg = 0
for _, pts in ipairs(TWIGS) do
  for i = 1, #pts-1 do
    local a, b = pts[i], pts[i+1]
    if math.max(a[1], b[1]) > 260 and math.min(a[1], b[1]) < 790 and math.max(a[2], b[2]) > 240 and math.min(a[2], b[2]) < 430 then
      local s = {a[1], a[2], b[1], b[2]}
      nseg = nseg + 1
      local x0, x1 = math.floor((math.min(a[1], b[1]) - 4)/GRID2), math.floor((math.max(a[1], b[1]) + 4)/GRID2)
      local y0, y1 = math.floor((math.min(a[2], b[2]) - 4)/GRID2), math.floor((math.max(a[2], b[2]) + 4)/GRID2)
      for gx = x0, x1 do
        for gy = y0, y1 do
          local k = gx*1000 + gy
          local c = gidx2[k]
          if not c then c = {}; gidx2[k] = c end
          c[#c+1] = s
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

  if x < 260 or x > 790 or y < 240 or y > 430 then return 0 end

  if not c then return 0 end
  for i = 1, #c do
    if segDist2(x, y, c[i]) <= 3.0 then return 1 end
  end
  return 0
end)

local function ribw(x0, y0, y1, w0, w1, wob, seed)
  local pts, ws = {}, {}
  local n = math.max(3, math.floor((y1-y0)/8))
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i/n
    pts[#pts+1] = {x0 + wob*math.sin(i*1.7 + seed) + rand(-0.5,0.5), y0 + (y1-y0)*t}
    ws[#ws+1] = w0 + (w1-w0)*math.sin(3.14*t)^0.7
  end
  return ribbon(pts, ws)
end

-- ===== soft wooded hills emerging from the fog: dry-on-dry stipple, crisp ragged tops, density falling downward and sideways =====
HillP  = pile{{"lead white",3.3},{"smalt",1.6},{"red earth",0.36},{"raw umber",0.14},{"Prussian blue",0.03}}
HillP2 = pile{{"lead white",2.7},{"smalt",1.8},{"red earth",0.34},{"raw umber",0.2},{"Prussian blue",0.05}}
function stipHill(pts, amp, seed, x0, x1, depth, p1, p2, strength)
  local topf = function(x) return interp(pts, x) + amp*trn(x*1.0 + seed, 3.0) end
  local m = mask(function(x,y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local t = topf(x)
    return smoothstep(t-0.5, t+0.5, y) * ((y < t + depth) and 1 or 0)
  end) - guardX - fgM - spAll - cliffM:grow(2)
  local side = function(x) return smoothstep(x0, x0 + 0.28*(x1-x0), x) * (1 - smoothstep(x1 - 0.28*(x1-x0), x1, x)) end
  local dens = function(x,y)
    local t = topf(x)
    local d = (y - t) / depth
    return strength * (1 - smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, d))^1.3 * side(x)
  end
  stipple(m, {pile=p1, width=3.2, coverage=function(x,y) return dens(x,y) end, feather=0.6, clip=m, pressure={0.35,0.8}, dips={30,0.9,0.3}, cluster=0.1})
  stipple(m, {pile=p2, width=2.2, coverage=function(x,y) return 0.8*dens(x,y)*(1 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.45, (y - topf(x))/depth)) end, feather=0.6, clip=m, pressure={0.35,0.8}, dips={30,0.9,0.3}, cluster=0.1})
  return m
end

-- ===== soft hills in the fog, dry-on-dry stipple that dissolves + a blend while it is open =====
clipHills = rect(-12, 395, 1030, 330) - fgM - guardAll - spAll - cliffM:grow(1.5)
function stipHill2(pts, amp, seed, depth, p1, p2, strength, gamma, fadeL, fadeR, xlo, xhi, tw1, tw2)
  local topf = function(x) return interp(pts, x) + amp*trn(x*1.0 + seed, 3.0) end
  local m = mask(function(x,y)
    if x < xlo or x > xhi then return 0 end
    local t = topf(x)
    return smoothstep(t-0.5, t+0.5, y) * ((y < t + depth) and 1 or 0)
  end) * clipHills
  local side = function(x)
    local l = fadeL and smoothstep(fadeL[1], fadeL[2], x) or 1
    local r = fadeR and (1 - smoothstep(fadeR[1], fadeR[2], x)) or 1
    return l * r
  end
  local dens = function(x,y)
    local t = topf(x)
    local d = (y - t) / depth
    return strength * (1 - smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, d))^(gamma or 1.3) * side(x)
  end
  stipple(m, {pile=p1, width=tw1 or 2.6, coverage=function(x,y) return dens(x,y) end, feather=0.6, clip=m, pressure={0.35,0.8}, dips={30,0.9,0.3}, cluster=0.1})
  stipple(m, {pile=p2, width=tw2 or 1.8, coverage=function(x,y) return 0.8*dens(x,y)*(1 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.5, (y - topf(x))/depth)) end, feather=0.6, clip=m, pressure={0.35,0.8}, dips={30,0.9,0.3}, cluster=0.1})
  blend(m:grow(3) * clipHills, {angle=0.0})
  blend(m:grow(3) * clipHills, {angle=0.03})
  return m
end

-- a hill that is a closed bump: its top profile reaches the fog level at both ends, so there is no vertical cut anywhere
function bumpHill(pts, amp, seed, depth, p1, p2, strength, gamma, tw1, tw2)
  local x0, x1 = pts[1][1], pts[#pts][1]
  local topf = function(x) return interp(pts, x) + amp*trn(x*1.0 + seed, 3.0) * smoothstep(x0, x0+30, x) * (1 - smoothstep(x1-30, x1, x)) end
  local m = mask(function(x,y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local t = topf(x)
    return smoothstep(t-0.5, t+0.5, y) * ((y < t + depth) and 1 or 0)
  end) * clipHills
  local dens = function(x,y)
    local t = topf(x)
    local d = (y - t) / depth
    local hh = clamp((pts[1][2] - t) / 40, 0, 1)    -- shallow near the ends: little paint where the bump meets the fog
    return strength * (1 - smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, d))^(gamma or 1.3) * hh^0.7
  end
  stipple(m, {pile=p1, width=tw1 or 2.6, coverage=function(x,y) return dens(x,y) end, feather=0.6, clip=m, pressure={0.35,0.8}, dips={30,0.9,0.3}, cluster=0.1})

  blend(m:grow(3) * clipHills, {angle=0.0})

function bumpHill2(pts, amp, seed, depth, p1, p2, strength, gamma, tw1, tw2, ybase)

My options are to wait for full drying and repaint the whole fog zone wet-in-wet, which would also bury the stippled hills, or accept the faint patches as minor imperfections. A better fix might be reshaping the hill density falloff itself so it fades to true zero at the edges through a steeper curve, avoiding the patch problem entirely rather than patching after the fact.

So the plan forming is: dry 14 days, rerun the fog coat to bury everything, dry again, then repaint the hills with the corrected falloff plus crowns and spire — costing one more painting cycle but the waits themselves are cheap. I'm also weighing whether to improve the fog coat itself this time, maybe adding subtle darker lilac billow shading to the flat cream half of the sea so it reads as atmospheric depth rather than empty space.

But I realize FogAll would bury the left-side hills too, since its boundary spans from far left. I'd need to restrict the new coat to the right region only, which risks reintroducing the same seam problem I had before at the boundary.

Actually, dissolving that hill edge into fog would look natural. Rather than redoing the whole fog coat, maybe it's simpler to fix the hill ends directly: since those patches read as cream-white against the pinkish-lilac-gray surroundings, a thin lilac glaze stippled over them with density fading outward would tone them down to match.

Though wet stippling over a not-fully-dry layer risks lifting and blending paint rather than cleanly glazing. Weighing whether to keep the arc hills at all — many Friedrich compositions thrive on large empty fog zones with the butte playing the role of an emerging peak, so skipping hills wouldn't ruin the composition, but I lean toward keeping them if I can get a natural shape.

Given how many tool calls I've already spent, I need to converge on a final minimal sequence: let the current layer dry, apply a fog coat on the right side blended from x=420 to preserve the left hills, dry again, then paint the right-side hills with proper zero-ended shapes, crowns, and the spire, and finish with a final review and closing note.

Before that, I'm also reconsidering the butte — it reads as a flat lilac-gray tabletop block with dark vertical fissures and a forested top, but it looks a bit like a cardboard cutout due to lacking light variation. I might add a glaze later to warm the lit face and darken the shaded side for more mountain-like depth.

Now I'm planning a second glaze pass on the dried butte, pushing stronger darkening across its right half down to roughly y=410 while adding warm light to the upper left, using a cool shadow mix of smalt, raw umber, Prussian blue, white, and red earth blended with medium, feathered along the shade edge.

I'm also layering a warm highlight glaze of red earth, ochre, white, and vermilion over the upper left corner, which should give the butte more solid rock-like contrast against the bright sky without pushing it too dark since it's a distant form. I'll apply this and check the result.

events.text: That glaze gave the cliff a streaky, mottled look, quite different from before. Let me step back and assess the whole piece.

events.name: look
events.text: size 1000

The cliff now looks like a streaky floating block, its base dropping below the fog line instead of sitting within it — the heavy glaze strokes seem to have painted over and erased the earlier haze and stipple work at the foot.

This was a mistake; I've overworked this butte and need to fix it with a fresh fog coat and a new cliff pass. Stepping back to assess the whole composition: the sky, oak, figure, and foreground all look solid, the fog sea with its hills mostly works though the mist-halo stippling looks a bit odd, but the butte itself is a clear problem that needs a different approach.

The real fix is waiting for the glaze to dry fully, then repainting the cliff with an opaque coat matching the earlier pale lilac-grey tones with a warm left side that had worked well before I added the streaky vertical glaze. I'm picturing what a good distant rock mass should look like in this style — bluish-grey, softly modeled with warm and cool sides, its base dissolving into mist like a tabletop rock emerging from fog.

That version was fine before adding the fissure ribs, which also worked well. The real fix is to just wait and re-coat the cliff fresh with the NB recipe rather than glazing — full blend plus foot stipple, same as the day-506 result, then leave it alone. I also need to deal with that faint vertical ghost edge around x≈545 on the left side.

I also notice a blotchy white halo near the right hills from the endFix stipple being too dense — it reads as patchy rather than smooth fog. Running the FogAll coat again after the cliff is finished should cover both the hills and smooth that out.

Actually, I'm reconsidering whether the hills belong at all. They give the fog sea some depth, but the two right-side arches look stiff and artificial compared to the calmer, emptier fog in the earlier evening version, which felt more like a Friedrich fog sea. A vast empty fog reads fine given the oak, butte, and spruces already carrying the composition, but maybe a few softer, more natural features would work better than the current rigid arches.

I'm thinking of swapping the arches for two or three small, irregular tree-topped knolls at different scales with soft, fading bases rather than hard edges. I've tried several approaches to get this naturalistic look — stippling worked decently except for hard vertical cuts at the ends, and the bump-based method closes those ends but still struggles with how the base blends into the fog.

Looking at the latest render, the hill reads like an arch with a flat-ish base — workable, but the white blotches around the endFix are bothering me, and the arch shape itself is too regular and wide. I'm mapping out a disciplined plan now: let everything dry fully, then re-coat the whole valley with a blended fog layer to bury the arch hills and blotches (while protecting the cliff's fog line), wait again, then redo the cliff separately.

For the final step, I'm thinking back to what worked on the left side — those hills used a closed bump-and-fade technique with crown dabs and conifer spikes that looked natural and irregular. I'll repeat that approach on the right with two smaller, asymmetrical hills instead of one wide regular arch, avoiding whatever caused the blotchy endFix issue.

I'm also weighing whether I actually need to wait out the full drying periods, or whether I can paint the fog coat over the valley now while the cliff glaze stays wet and protected by the mask — though I need to check whether the cliff's foot area, which gets included in the fog coat region, is actually dry enough yet.

The blotchy hills still look tacky since they were painted only a few hours ago, so recoating now risks ghosting; better to commit to a full 16-day wait before the fog coat step. I'm considering combining the fog and cliff coat steps into one session after a single wait, since the fog coat's mask should already exclude the cliff region.

Actually painting the cliff foot wet-in-wet with the fog coat could work well since the lowest cliff band's color matches the fog color, letting them merge seamlessly without a visible seam—similar to how the day 506 recoat turned out.

So concretely: wait 16 days, redo the full fog coat (excluding the cliff above the footline) and blend it, then immediately recoat the cliff's NB bands with blending, matching the foot band to the fog color, followed by a light stipple near the foot. Once dry, I can properly add the right knolls dry-on-dry and finish up.

I need the foot to dissolve into the fog while the cliff gains real structure: a darker bluish shadow side, warm lit left, fissures, and a tree line on top. Since adding anything wet-in-wet now would just soften further, I'm planning to wait for this layer to dry, then build form with dry-brush vertical strokes using a small filbert loaded lightly with shadow color — broken color that reads as rock texture rather than a pasted-on streak, aiming for a mid-value tone just slightly darker than the fog.

I'm mapping out vertical bands across the cliff's width: a lit pinnacle, a mid-tone main body, a dark gully, a darker turret, and a shaded right shoulder, with full contrast concentrated in the upper portion and the lower part fading into haze toward the fog.

I want to apply these bands as unblended vertical strokes so the texture survives, with paint load fading with height so the transition stays within similar cliff colors. Before that though, I need to fix the foot boundary by stippling in a fog density ramp near the base, similar to an approach that worked previously.

Since the cliff is now wet, stippling there will let the paint lift and fuse into the wash, which is what I want for dissolving the foot. I'll do three wet passes, then a low-coverage "edge=lost" fog to soften the very bottom, then let it dry before moving to dry-brush modeling.

Assessing the composition honestly now: the sky gradient works well, the oak reads as a strong silhouette though a bit flat and Friedrich-like, the figure is appropriately small, and the butte has become a soft hazy distant form that's slightly lumpy but acceptable.

The fog sea is smooth but has a stray ghostly vertical edge around x≈540, and I realize my latest fog recoat accidentally buried the left-side hills too, not just fixed the right half as intended — leaving that whole left valley flat and empty when it needed some texture for depth. The foreground dark hill with gold grass and the lower-right spruces are both holding up fine.

Looking closer at the left, I can still make out a faint lilac hill area and traces of hill C beneath the fog, but it's thinner and emptier than before. Given how many sessions this has taken and that each fog coat demands a long wait, I think the smart move now is to add any remaining hill features in one final pass that nothing gets recoated over afterward — bringing back something like the wooded hill C with dark conifer crowns that looked good in an earlier version, to ground the lower-left corner.

For the right side, I want to redo the stiff, artificial-looking arches as a set of smaller, irregular wooded knolls of varying size and distance instead — asymmetrical profiles with uneven tree clusters on top, using fewer sweeps of the hill brush to avoid the halo and arch problems from before.

Looking back at hill C, that result read as a genuinely convincing wooded hill in the fog, with just a minor hard edge near where the profile meets the oak roots — overall fine. I want to replicate that same crown-dab technique for the right side, building three closed bumps with scattered crown dabs similar to C.

I'm sketching coordinates for two main knolls (K1 around x=560-760, K2 around x=850-1012) plus a smaller K3 bump near x=790, each with slightly asymmetric peaked profiles. I'm also considering adding a tiny distant church spire on K1, a Friedrich-style touch — a small silhouette with a pointed roof nestled in the mist to add narrative depth and a sense of scale.

Placing it around x~650, y~488 keeps it below the glow line and set against pale fog rather than open sky, creating a visual chain where the viewer's eye moves from the figure to the spire to the distant butte — subtle, dark lilac rather than black to suggest atmospheric distance, about 22 units tall. Given the modest cost of adding each hill, I'm planning to tackle the whole composition in one session, starting with the left hill.

Actually, before committing to that, I should take a closer look at what's currently in the left portion of the scene.

The left fog shows some faint crosshatch texture from repeated blending, but at full scale it just reads as a subtle textured mist, which works fine. Now I'm moving on to add the left wooded hill using bumpHill2 again, plus the right side.

I'm checking whether to include a hazy lilac ridge at the left too — looking at the image, there are faint lilac ridges around that region, good enough as is. I'll repaint hill C, reusing the global masks that persisted through the rebuild, but I want to dial back the fog strength a bit since the lower band came out too heavy last time — dropping strength from 11 to 9 and depth to 80.

For the right side, I'm laying out smaller, more varied knolls with lighter crown dabs since they're farther away: one rounded hill spanning roughly x=560–795 cresting near y=493, a second further right around x=860–1030, and a possible smaller closer knoll around x=770–915 with darker fill, though I might skip that third one to avoid making the knolls look too repetitive. I'm also placing a thin spire tower rising above the first knoll's crest near x=650.

I'm sketching the spire in a muted lilac-dark tone, plus a couple of tiny roof shapes flanking it to suggest a distant village peeking through the mist—something like Friedrich's small church towers in his misty landscapes. It feels like it could add charm without overdoing it, so I'll keep it subtle and soft, then move on to finish hill C and see how it reads.

events.text:
I'm noticing the hills still show hard vertical edges at their ends because the stipple density depends on vertical distance from the top, which doesn't fade to zero near the mask boundaries — I need to add horizontal falloff near the edges too.

So that lingering density at the arch ends creates a visible vertical lilac edge. I'm thinking the fix is to multiply the density by a smooth x-envelope that fades to zero near the start and end of each arch, rather than cutting it off hard — which is the approach the earlier fade-based attempt used with some success.

Maybe the blend step is the culprit—since it lifts and drags paint within its mask boundary, buildup could occur right at the mask edge even without leaking outside it. I'm also noticing a darker vertical rim near the right end of K1 in the bumpHill2 image, suggesting this isn't isolated to one hill.

To fix this, I'll drop the blend step and use an x-envelope to taper density to zero at the arch ends instead, accepting that stipple dots stay visible as fine grain (unnoticeable at full scale). But both K1 and K2 still have vertical sides needing coverage, and attempts to fix the ends with a cream stipple color created blotchy halos because the local fog color shifts with lilac noise shading, making an exact match difficult without another full coat.

Extending the hill profiles into sloping tails wouldn't remove the vertical cut where the mass ends, and a uniform cream glaze would only reduce contrast rather than hide the edge — I need a different approach to make these edges disappear entirely.

Since this paint is still wet, I could stipple the surrounding fog color directly over the vertical edge while it's fresh, letting the colors fuse and dissolve the boundary — unlike the earlier case where the hills had already dried before I attempted an edge fix.

That earlier fix produced blotchy halos because the stipple color was lighter and warmer than the local fog. -- ===== the grey skirt: covered with fog-coloured stipple, density falling off smoothly 30 units beyond it =====
function sdRect(x, y, x0, y0, x1, y1)
  local cx, cy = (x0+x1)/2, (y0+y1)/2
  local hx, hy = (x1-x0)/2, (y1-y0)/2
  local dx, dy = math.abs(x-cx) - hx, math.abs(y-cy) - hy
  local ox, oy = math.max(dx,0), math.max(dy,0)
  return math.sqrt(ox*ox+oy*oy) + math.min(math.max(dx,dy),0)
end
skirtM = rect(655, 376, 310, 130) - fgM - guardX

  local d = sdRect(x, y, 702, 406, 918, 464)
  local ring = 1 - smoothstep(0, 30, d)
  local top = smoothstep(390, 412, y)
  return 8.0 * ring * top
end

**The Old Oak above the Fog**

A vast bare oak stands on a dark crest at the left. Its crooked boughs and fine twigs are drawn against a sky that grades from smalt blue through pale green and lemon to peach at the horizon. A small man in a dark coat, seen from behind with a staff, stands under its low right bough and looks out over a sea of fog. The afterglow is a long low band behind the fog, and a few thin cloud bars and birds cross the sky above it.

Far to the right a rock mesa rises out of the mist with a warm lit edge and a dark wooded crown. A small wooded knoll shows in the fog nearby. Three spruces stand at the lower right and balance the oak. The dark foreground is rim-lit with dry grass.

I painted it slowly in thin layers, letting each dry before the next, on a warm ochre ground under pale lead white. The sky, mist and distances are soft and smooth; the oak and the figure are crisp dark silhouettes. Two things I'd still change: the mesa reads a little pasted-on, and the fog sea on the right is flat.

For the fog sea, I'm thinking about adding subtle horizontal banding with dry stipple and soft edges—cooler lilac tones nearer the viewer and warmer light near the horizon to create recession, since the right portion currently reads too flat and uniformly cream.

The lower right spruces work fine as framing elements, but the lower left foreground is a large dark empty area that could use more content given how Friedrich typically handles such spaces.

For the tree trunk, it's rendered mostly as flat dark silhouette, which makes sense since the oak is backlit against the afterglow at the horizon — the sun source is clearly to the right of the tree, so a subtle warm rim light on the trunk's right edge would reinforce that lighting logic.

The sky reads clean but a bit flat at the top; Friedrich's skies usually have richer gradation, though the thin stratus clouds at right work fine. I'm weighing whether the painting I judged complete at day 673 truly needs more work — the mesa feels like the weakest element and the right half still feels empty, but I want to be careful not to repeat past mistakes while trying to push the piece toward the best version I can make.

For the right side, I'm thinking the mesa should sit smaller and more distant with a blue-violet aerial-perspective tone, and have a more distinctive sandstone silhouette — flat top, vertical walls, a slight overhang and notch — rather than its current blobby three-lobed shape, with its base dissolving softly into fog for better depth.

Reshaping risks halos if I try to carve the old silhouette away with sky-colored stippling, so painting an opaque new shape over it that's larger than the original might be safer, though that makes it feel closer and more dominant. I'm weighing whether it's better to instead reduce it by carving back into the sky's gradient, which shifts from lemon tones higher up to peach and gold lower down near the mesa.

Actually, the simpler fix might be keeping the existing silhouette but addressing specific flaws — like that pale lilac halo ring around the edge that reads as a cutout border rather than natural haze. I could try painting a thin cool-violet stroke along the mesa's edge to extend it outward and absorb that ring, rather than trying to erase it with sky color.

Then there's the right lobes reading like ears, which I could fix by glazing them lighter and reshaping, and the foot where ragged dark stipple looks like debris instead of a clean fog transition. Maybe the better move is adding structural rock features — vertical fissures, strata lines, a few tiny trees — to make the mesa read more convincingly as stone, so I want to zoom into the mid-level region to study the real details before deciding.

Zooming in, the mesa reads as a ghost-like castle form: a pinkish speckled left spire, a flat unmodelled lilac-grey body, darker speckled right lobes with an odd arch-like "doorway" patch and a strange light halo. It's Friedrich-like and passable but still feels pasted-on, so I'm thinking the real improvement needs to come from giving the fog sea more atmospheric body rather than just fixing the mesa itself.

Right now there's a huge flat cream void on the right side of the composition that's the single emptiest area in the whole painting, which feels like a real compositional weakness compared to how Friedrich handles similar fog scenes with emerging ridgelines and lit bands.

I'm considering treating this emptiness deliberately as "vastness" rather than a flaw, though the lozenge shape is still a problem. I'm also looking at the fog-to-sky border near the top and whether it reads convincingly, and thinking about a low-risk fix using a thin dry lilac glaze over a soft noise-based mask to add subtle modulation without over-painting.

events.text:
I've put around 450 chunks into this mesa and it's become a strange blob at this point. I'm weighing whether to stop here with the title and description or push for one more real improvement, since being "back at the easel" seems to invite another look despite my last note saying "finished."

Evaluating it like a viewer would: the oak, sky, and crest work well, the figure is fine, but the mesa reads oddly—like a castle on a cloud with unconvincing ear-like lobes—while the fog's lozenge shape is a clear flaw. I'm thinking about how Friedrich handled distant rock massifs in works like "Der Watzmann" or "Das Eismeer" to figure out what would make this element more convincing.

A low-risk fix could be adding thin, graded horizontal fog wisps crossing the mesa's lower third, which would break up the blobby silhouette and integrate it with the fog by splitting it into a visible crown above and a softened foot below.

Actually, maybe the better plan is to repaint the mesa as a fresh object entirely, since it's been so reworked already. Given the sunset glow at right of center, the mesa's left face should catch warm light while the right stays in blue shadow, with a dark wooded crown on top — the existing design has the right idea but lumpy execution. Still, stepping back, the painting reads cohesively at normal viewing distance.

The mesa's silhouette against the sky is the strongest shape besides the oak, reading clearly as a rock massif, with the ghosting and halo barely visible at thumbnail scale. Thinking about the overall composition — the oak and figure at left, the open "sea of fog" vista at right, balanced laterally by the mesa and the three spruces at lower right — it forms a diagonal flow from the oak down to the spruces, a classic compositional arrangement.

The remaining flaws, a blobby mesa and a lozenge-shaped fog patch, feel minor against the painting's overall success, so I'm weighing a cautious plan to touch up the weakest areas using only thin, dry, soft-edged scumbled layers on a fully dried surface, carefully guarding the tree, twigs, figure, and spruces, with no blending at all — starting with modulating the fog sea in the lower right portion of the canvas.

First I need to crop in at 1:1 on that lighter oval patch around x 700-945, y 400-490, since its soft right edge and darker band below suggest it needs closer inspection before I decide how to adjust it. I'm planning a gentle gradient across the fog, cooler and lilac near the bottom, cream in the middle, warm near the horizon, plus a few low fog bank wisps with lost edges, and separately a soft horizontal veil band across the mesa's lower-middle to add tonal separation.

For the trunk, I'm considering a thin warm rim light on the right edge of the trunk and larger limbs, but I'm second-guessing it since the trunk sits against a bright cream sky glow on the left -- a backlit rim wouldn't realistically show up against a background that's brighter than the rim itself.

For the foreground, the dark slope reads too flat; I should add variation like scattered stones, a faint path, thistles, and a touch of raking light along the crest to match Friedrich's detailed dark foregrounds, beyond just the grass blades already there.

Before making changes, I want to inspect each region at full resolution: the trunk, the lower foreground, the fog area, the figure, and the spruces.

I'm examining the fog region closely, noticing a hard vertical edge from a lighter lozenge shape, horizontal wipe streaks, a lilac mid band, and a small knoll with conifer tips poking through the mist.

In the trunk crop, I notice a subtle pale lilac halo outlining the dark limbs against the bright sky — likely a feathered boundary left from the repaint where the guard mask grew slightly beyond the limb edges, leaving a thin ring of old paint color visible. It's a soft, cutout-like effect that's barely noticeable in the full picture.

I'm also looking at the left hill with its conifer-topped ridge and the fog-lilac valley beneath it.

The trunk itself reads too flat right now, lacking the rugged bark texture Friedrich's oaks typically show — I'm thinking of adding subtle vertical furrows in lighter warm umber with darker fissures to model it like a cylinder catching rim light from the afterglow on its right side, since the paint there has had plenty of time to dry.

Separately, the mist's visible edge at x~940 is still a problem — my past attempts at fixing that boundary with dry stippling have ended up blotchy, so I need a cleaner approach there.

For the broader fog sea, a full wet-in-wet recoat worked cleanly on day 535 but got damaged by later hill work, and subsequent attempts on day 566 and others left artifacts like the "ghost rectangle." Redoing a full FogAll coat now risks burying the mesa foot, knoll, and horizon strip, meaning I'd have to redo a lot of adjacent work just to restore one boundary.

I think structure would serve better than another flat coat — maybe a distant lilac ridge of low hills with faint tree-lines along the right horizon around x=880-1000, breaking up the flat fog top. Friedrich's fog seas typically have an undulating horizon rather than a dead-flat line with just a mesa sitting on it, so introducing that kind of variation could feel more natural.

Actually, rather than adding new ridges, I should focus on quieting the mesa itself — its darkest lobe (~100-130 value) is too strong against the lighter fog (~225) and competes with the oak for attention. Lightening and hazing it would push it back and reinforce the sense of depth without adding any new elements.

Given that dry-on-dry stippling has worked reliably, I'll settle on a short list of guarded tweaks: refining the trunk's bark texture and adding a faint warm rim light on its right edge and root flare, staying strictly within the trunk mask. I need to locate the right mask name among the 1116 globals, but with 6587 lines in the log and no grep capability, scanning the whole file would be too costly in tokens.

Instead I can query Lua directly by iterating over `_G` and filtering global names containing keywords like 'trunk', 'tree', 'oak', 'guard', or 'twig'. Beyond that, I'm planning to fix the fog sea lozenge's right edge with a thin lilac glaze, and ease the mesa's contrast and pale halo slightly with a crossing fog veil band, though I'll wait for the current layer to dry before applying anything new.

Still thinking through composition: the foreground needs some richness, maybe a few boulders at lower left with subtle warm light, but first I want to check it at 1:1 along with the figure and the sky to see the whole picture.

Looking closer at the foreground texture, I notice the grass is rendered as repetitive golden hooked arcs over near-black earth. I also spot a pale-lilac halo around the oak's twig tips, suggesting an older layer of paint showing through.

The figure's silhouette with the staff reads well and needs no change. For improvement, I'm thinking of adding a few taller dry stalks or seedheads rising above the crest between x 450–800, silhouetted against the pale fog, to break the repetitive grass pattern and echo Friedrich's detailed foreground plants—though these dark stems against light fog would need careful, sparing rigger work to avoid looking heavy-handed.

Beyond that, the right-side fog could use subtle tonal modulation, the mesa edge could be softened, and the trunk's modeling deepened—since the trunk is the largest dark mass and main subject, that's likely the highest-impact fix, with the fog and mesa close behind and the stalks as a lower-priority nicety. Before committing time to any of this, I want to check what masks and guards already exist—things like the twig polylines, tree mask, guard regions, foreground mask, and figure mask—so I should print out the global names to see what's available.

Squinting at the image, I can see the problem clearly now: a visible rounded-rectangle lozenge of lighter cream fog with a defined edge, like a paper label stuck on the fog, likely a leftover outline from the skirt stipple coverage pass. The mesa reads as a gray-purple block with a darker lobe, almost like a cloud or castle shape.

I'm deciding to fix the lozenge by applying a thin veil of fog-lilac over the whole area plus its surroundings, using a smooth stipple gradient with no hard edges so the boundary melts into the overall fog gradient instead of standing out as a flaw.

A smooth veil ramp wouldn't cancel a sharp edge step — I'd need the veil to follow the lozenge's exact contour with a matching step, which is the same crisp-seam problem as before and hard to pin down without inspecting actual pixel boundaries.

Alternatively, I could cover the seam with a wide stippled scumble in the in-between tone, ramping coverage up and down across the boundary band so the hard edge dissolves into two softer transitions. This is essentially a pointillist broken-colour blend — stippling the lighter tone over the darker side and vice versa, each with density falling off away from the seam, which could produce a genuinely smooth gradient instead of a visible step.

I can work out the coverage fractions on each side so the blended means match exactly at the seam, turning the hard tonal boundary into a continuous gradient instead of a visible edge.

I need the actual L and S paint piles matched to the existing fog colors, but I don't have a way to sample pixel values directly from the canvas. I'll have to match by eye instead, maybe by painting test swatches somewhere and comparing — like the earlier PfA/PfB/PfC stipple test patches I placed near the lozenge's left edge.

Actually, I think I've found the cause: my own skirt-covering stipple used PfB, a lighter cream than the surrounding fog, applied over a rounded-rectangle region with a 30-unit falloff ramp — that's exactly what's creating the lozenge shape.

I should soften that edge by widening the ramp considerably or reducing contrast against the surround, maybe stippling the lozenge's color to blend with the lilac fog, or washing the whole region with a gentler, wider gradient so its boundaries dissolve into the horizon rather than forming a visible rim. Alternatively, I could extend a very slow, wide cream glow outward from the lozenge over ~120 units so it reads as the brightest point within a broader luminous field rather than an isolated shape.

Since the real light source sits in the sky near the horizon around x~600-700, the fog there should naturally glow brightest and fade toward the viewer and sides -- so a smooth radial gradient centered near (700, 410) makes more physical sense than a hard-edged lozenge. I'm considering replacing the lozenge with that radial glow, using a Gaussian-like density ramp roughly 150 units wide so any residual step from the original paint gets absorbed into the continuous gradient rather than standing out as an edge.

This gives a smooth feathered gradient rather than a hard edge, turning the lozenge into a luminous glow with a long skirt—the fine stipple granularity and density ramp should stay visually negligible. I'm confirming this is meant to cover the grey skirt area under the mesa with fog-coloured stipple, consistent with my earlier plan.

Checking the rest of the log, it seems the last worked chunk was 448 and the journal marks day 673 as finished, so I'm now laying out next steps: wait for everything to dry (roughly 10-14 days to be safe), then fix the lozenge using a wide-ramp dry-on-dry stipple while carefully excluding the twigs, spruces, mesa, and crest foreground regions.

I'm weighing whether extending the stipple skirt around the lozenge risks bleeding into the crest or spruce areas nearby, and second-guessing whether adding more stipple texture to the fog is even the right move given the existing brush-stroke texture already visible there.

That lighter halo ring around the right lobe seems to be where the neighboring sky paint bleeds through against the dark silhouette. I could fix this by painting a thin darker outline along the mesa's edge in its local tone using the detail brush, though I need to be careful near the top edge where it catches the light.

My fix list for the mesa: remove the halo ring on the right lobes by stippling over it with the lobe's tone, soften its contrast against the fog with a few horizontal dry-scumbled wisps that fade at the ends, and maybe add 2-3 short dark-violet fissure lines near the crown for rock texture without overdoing it into a barcode pattern.

Before adding anything new, I should let the mesa and skirt dry — maybe 20 days given the tackiness near (800,350) from the latest paint chunk. Dry-on-dry stippling over tacky paint should still work fine since the dabs will grab rather than blend, which is what I want to avoid. I'll also take another look at how the trunk reads before continuing.

The trunk currently reads as flat and uniform, so I want to add bark texture — gnarled, wavy vertical strokes with warm brown highlights in Friedrich's style to give it more dimension.

I'm figuring out which trunk should be lit warm on the right and cool on the left, with fissure lines and furrows where the trunk splits into limbs near the top. Before painting I want to inspect the trunk masks by sampling coordinates to map their shapes, since I can't easily grep the log for their definitions.

I notice there's a faint pale lilac halo ringing the limbs where I recoated the sky — leftover old sky color showing as a guard band against the new sky. It's barely visible at normal viewing size, so I'll leave it alone rather than try to fix it.

Stepping back, the overall composition does read as Friedrich-like: bare oak against the afterglow, lone figure, sea of fog, and the sky gradient feels smooth with just a couple of faint cloud wisps. Now I'm weighing whether to enrich the empty right half with a low-risk addition, like a distant ridge strip along the horizon.

Actually I think I'll leave that right side alone, since the existing fog band and peach-colored sky above it already read fine without extra ridge detail. My practical sequence is to tackle the lozenge fix first, then unify the mesa tones with added wisps, then refine the trunk bark, then maybe the stalks—checking after each dry stipple pass since they're all reversible by overpainting if something looks worse. Before moving forward though, I want to reconsider whether that lozenge issue might stem from a different underlying cause.

Tracing it back, the rounded-corner outline I'm seeing in the squint view actually comes from the sdRect ring effect, where the distance-based ramp from the rectangle edge creates those soft rounded corners through the Euclidean falloff and feathering — the coverage naturally fades below full opacity past a certain distance threshold.

Inside the lozenge where ring is at max, I get solid coverage with the light cream fill, while the narrow band near the edge is where it drops off sharply due to the smoothstep curve, creating that crisp rim effect over just a few units of distance. The fix would be widening that ramp with a better smoothing function to soften the transition.

Computing the replacement percentages along this gradient — roughly 93% at d=26, 55% at d=60, 27% at d=100, and 10% at d=150 — it forms a smooth ~100-unit-wide halo transitioning from the lozenge color to the surround color with no visible edge. I'm second-guessing whether the exponential coverage formula is right for stipple dabs versus random fills, since stipple coverage depends on touches per point rather than random dab overlap.

With a dab width of 3.2, each touch covers about 5.1 square units, so coverage fraction still follows a Poisson-style 1-exp(-c) relationship, and at a 5% value difference with 3-unit scale the speckle pattern should be nearly invisible. I'm also noting the surround isn't uniform — there are lilac horizontal bands around y~500-520 that complicate the blend.

The glow around the mesa foot may extend into that lilac band, lightening it slightly, which actually works well: the overall composition has bright creamy fog near the horizon leading the eye up to the mesa, the lilac band providing mid-ground recession, and a lighter zone near the bottom right, with the lightest lozenge sitting right under the mesa foot. A smooth radial glow there reads naturally as atmospheric haze around the mesa, so I'll keep that rather than darkening the lozenge. Now I should move to thinking about how to knit together the mesa itself.

The speckled texture on the right lobe is what reads as dirty; I could try a fine uniform stipple to smooth it while keeping slight tonal variation, though past attempts turned grainy. Maybe it's better to just accept the mottled mass since the grain only shows at high zoom, and instead address the blob-like silhouette by adding small crags or notches along the flat top edge.

Painting a few small rock needles in the lilac body tone above the conifer row — between roughly x 770-820, each 6-14 units tall with a lit left edge — would break up the skyline and evoke the jagged Elbe Sandstone "Felsnadeln" look, strengthening the Friedrich-like character.

A thin fog wisp crossing the mesa's mid-body, cream-colored with soft lost edges, would occlude part of it and visually integrate it as if seen through mist. I'm planning to render this with a stippled dot pattern, density peaking along a wavy central band and thinning toward the feathered edges.

To avoid a speckled halo look, I'll use two passes with a finer width near the thin edges, and test the technique cautiously at low density before committing to the mesa, since the cream color needs to match the surrounding fog. I'm also weighing an alternative glaze-stroke approach using a dissolving mask for the wisp's edge.

I should match the veil's tint to the warm cream of the fog rather than letting it read white or cold. Moving to the trunk and limbs, I'm thinking about adding subtle modelling since real oak limbs aren't pure flat silhouettes — maybe a warm rim of glow light along the right edge of the trunk to break the flatness.

For the bark treatment itself, I'm planning a warm brown rim, vertical furrow strokes done dry, and a touch of cool reflected light on the left side. Before adding these, I want to check the existing bark texture layers already in place.

local function edgeAt(m, y, x0, x1)
  local prev = m:at(x0, y)
  for x = x0, x1, 0.5 do
    local v = m:at(x, y)
    if (prev > 0.5) ~= (v > 0.5) then return x end
    prev = v
  end
  return nil
end

  local out = {}

  return table.concat(out, " ")

Weighing whether a complete recoat justifies the cost in sessions and tokens at day 714 — a full recoat would erase the ghost rectangle artifact and smooth the fog sea, but it would also bury the knoll and require repainting it along with the mesa foot, while the spruces stay protected by their own mask.

A cheaper alternative occurs to me: a light dry-on-dry stipple veil across the whole fog region with a smooth ramp at its left and bottom edges, which would homogenize tone and push the knoll further into the distance without fully erasing the ghost edges. Looking at the right side in value mode at full scale, the ghost artifact under the mesa reads as a faint pedestal of denser fog with subtle lighter bands at its edges — at whole-image scale this is subtle enough that it might actually be acceptable to leave mostly as-is.

But I notice the straight vertical and bottom edges are the giveaway, so the fix is to break them with soft, irregular horizontal wisps of varying length crossing those sides at different heights, interrupting the geometric regularity so it reads as natural mist drift instead.

Actually a stronger fix would be painting a distinct fog bank layer: a long, low horizontal cloud crossing in front of the mesa's base, roughly x~640-1000, with a gently wavy, feathered upper edge around y~405-415 that dissolves softly at the bottom, reading as a deliberate atmospheric layer rather than a leftover rectangle.

Stepping back, I'm trying to think about first impressions of the whole piece — the oak silhouette, the figure, the glowing sky, the dark hill, the fog, and the distant mesa that currently reads a bit like a cartoonish cliff castle. The stippled curtain at the mesa's foot is part of what gives it that overly fussy texture, so that's probably where to focus next.

Actually, the bigger fix might be the mesa's shape and color entirely — making it read like genuine Elbe sandstone with vertical faces, stratification, a treed flat top, and talus slopes at the base, bathed in cool blue-violet haze with a warm-lit left edge. Right now it's a flat mauve slab with an odd rounded bulb on the upper right and a salmon column, with no real strata — that bulb is clearly a leftover artifact from an earlier version of the cliff outline that needs reshaping into something straighter and flatter.

Though reworking the silhouette risks disturbing the smooth wet-in-wet sky blend, I think the irregular profile is passable as a rock mass — it could read like Lilienstein's flat-topped block or one of Friedrich's pointed crags. Adding a few thin, slightly wavy horizontal bedding lines across the lit face would likely do more for realism than reshaping the whole form.

Since the mesa is fully dry now (last work on it was long enough ago), I can safely add dry-on-dry strata detail with the rigger — thin, low-opacity dark mauve lines running horizontally across the face and thickening toward the shade side, plus a few vertical cracks dropping from the top that fade out downward.

This texture should break up the "blob" feel and sell the rock structure at the right scale, though I need to be careful it reads as sedimentary ledges rather than scratches — using low-pressure strokes with natural thinning, a slightly darker shade-mixed color, light waviness, and maybe a thin lit edge below each dark line to suggest a ledge catching light. Given how small the mesa is on screen, the line weight needs to stay restrained.

I'm also reconsidering the vertical streaking at the mesa's foot — that drip-like stipple pattern looks more like virga than a soft diffuse base shadow, so I need a dry-on-dry remedy, maybe a horizontal scumble pass to blend the pale gaps rather than letting the streaks stay vertical.

Actually, viewed in context it reads as mist boiling around the rock base, which feels natural — I'll leave it as is. The remaining priorities are the mesa's strata and fissures, rim lighting on the trunk and major limbs, fixing the ghost wisps, and final touches — with the trunk's rim light being especially important since the oak is the focal point and its lighting ties it to the sky, similar to how Friedrich handles his oaks.

Friedrich tends to render oaks as dark silhouettes with minimal modeling, so a strong rim light isn't necessary — maybe just a faint warm sheen along the right edge to suggest volume, applied with sparse, feathered stippling in warm dark brown, concentrated on the right portion of the trunk and limbs and fading leftward. I want to check that this rim direction actually matches where the sun is positioned below the horizon.

Since the glow sits behind and to the right of the oak, the trunk's right edge would catch that raking light while the limbs' upper surfaces might pick up a cooler sky tone — though that's probably too subtle to bother with, so I'll stick to just the trunk edge and maybe the right-facing limb surfaces. Now I'm shifting to think through the ghost figure and how to work out what visually distinguishes its interior from its surroundings.

Zooming into the lozenge shape's left edge, I'm tracing exactly where the pale vertical bands sit relative to the darker interior and the outside fog — identifying those pale columns beside the "legs" as a lighter stipple effect distinct from both the lozenge's dark core and the ambient fog tone.

I'll stipple T_m with dense coverage fading outward over the columns, since the earlier attempt with lighter coverage only partially fixed it. Comparing colors, the columns actually match the surrounding fog cream tone fine—it's the lozenge interior that reads greyer, so that's really the mismatch I need to address.

Tracing the grey patch's vertical edges, they line up exactly with my blockD rectangle (729-881 with a 24-unit ramp) plus the leg boxes added afterward, so the pale columns are just leftover fog between those passes. The cleanest fix is probably widening the ramp around the grey patch with a soft, low-density ring of the same T_m tone to blend the edge better.

If I stretch the smoothstep ramp out to 80-90 units instead of 24, the patch stops reading as a boxed-in shape and instead becomes a gentle shadow pooling under the mesa's foot, which feels natural rather than ghostly. I'm setting up the stipple region with a distance function from a rectangular core and a vertical profile to taper the effect smoothly.

The pale-lilac veil color will darken the existing grey patch slightly while softening its edge contrast, and it'll also help blend the bright pale columns into their surroundings. I think doing this soft veil first is the safe move since it's a dry-on-dry layer, then I'll tackle the strata detail and rim light afterward — though I'm pausing to consider whether darkening the fog near the mesa's base is actually the right atmospheric choice.

I'll simplify that into a soft lilac veil rather than a hard stretch. Checking the fog values — light grey around 0.85 against the mesa's mid-tones near 0.5-0.6 — and confirming the overall Friedrich feel: the cool-to-warm palette, the silhouetted oak, and the figure seen from behind all read true. Moving forward with this.

function stalk(x0, h, lean, p, pr, headLen)
  local yb = crestY(x0) + 5
  local pts = {}
  local n = 6
  local ph = rand(0, 6.28)
  for i = 0, n do
    local t = i / n
    local x = x0 + lean * h * (t^1.7) + 0.6 * math.sin(ph + t*5.0) * t
    local y = yb - h * t
    pts[#pts+1] = {x, y}
  end
  stalkB:reload(p, 1.0)
  stalkB:stroke(pts, {pressure={pr, pr*0.75, pr*0.55}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  if headLen and headLen > 0 then
    local tx, ty = pts[#pts][1], pts[#pts][2]
    local px, py = pts[#pts-1][1], pts[#pts-1][2]
    local dx, dy = tx - px, ty - py
    local dl = math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy)
    dx, dy = dx/dl, dy/dl
    stalkB:reload(p, 1.0)
    stalkB:stroke({{tx - dx*0.5, ty - dy*0.5}, {tx + dx*headLen*0.5, ty + dy*headLen*0.5}, {tx + dx*headLen, ty + dy*headLen}}, {pressure={0.75, 0.9, 0.35}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  end
end

    local t = i / n
    local phi = phi0 + k * (t ^ 1.8) + 0.05 * math.sin(ph + t * 6.0)
    local ds = L / n
    dirx, diry = math.sin(phi), -math.cos(phi)
    x = x + dirx * ds
    y = y + diry * ds
    pts[#pts+1] = {x, y}
  end
  fineB2:reload(p, 1.0)
  fineB2:stroke(pts, {pressure={pr0 or 0.5, (pr0 or 0.5) * 0.7, 0.14}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  if head and head > 0 then
    local tx, ty = pts[#pts][1], pts[#pts][2]
    fineB2:reload(p, 1.0)
    fineB2:stroke({{tx - dirx*1.0, ty - diry*1.0}, {tx + dirx*head*0.5, ty + diry*head*0.5}, {tx + dirx*head, ty + diry*head}}, {pressure={0.55, 0.75, 0.2}, ramps={0.0, 0.0}})
  end
  return pts
end

function tentY(y, c, wu, wd)

bandsF = {

function fogBandCov(i, kind)
  local b = bandsF[i]
  return function(x, y)
    local hm = smoothstep(-0.05, 0.30, nBandA(x * 1.0 + i * 91, i * 37)) * smoothstep(b.x0, b.x0 + 70, x)
    local wob = 4.0 * nBandB(x, i * 53)
    local yy = y - wob
    if kind == "shade" then
      local u = (yy - (b.c + 0.2*b.h)) / b.h
      return 2.4 * math.exp(-u*u) * hm
    else
      local u = (yy - (b.c - 0.9*b.h)) / (0.55*b.h)
      return 1.6 * math.exp(-u*u) * hm
    end
  end
end

**Title: *The Oak above the Sea of Fog* (Eiche über dem Nebelmeer)**

At dusk a huge bare oak stands on a dark heath crest at the left. Its crooked boughs and roughly 1,400 twigs spread against a sky that runs from smalt blue at the top through cream-green and lemon to peach at the horizon. A small man in a dark coat, seen from behind and leaning on a staff, stands under its low right bough. He looks out over a fog-filled valley.

On the far right a rock mesa lit by the afterglow rises out of the mist. It has a warm left edge, a violet shadow side and a dark wooded crown. Its foot dissolves into the fog. A small wooded knoll sits in the mist below it. In the foreground, rim-lit dry grasses and a few tall stalks catch the last light, and three dark spruces frame the lower right.

A few things I'd still change. The mesa is soft and a little smudgy up close. The fog sea on the right is calm and nearly empty. Faint pale fringes remain at some twig tips and under the low limb, left where the fog stopped short of the guarded branches.

Compose and paint one original landscape in the manner of Caspar David
